idea.title: Remove the repeated step push at rounds 9 and later
idea.summary: At 16 rounds every round past the 8th re-adds step_emb row 7 to all 17 controller vectors while the norm grows about 4 per round, none of which training saw. Zero-training hooks test the step addition (removed, replaced by the mean row, or index reset for a second look), magnitude held at the round-8 size, and drift removal, split into no-program and program rows because the whole drop sits in no-program rows. The prior that the clamp is the main cause is low.
idea.change: Forward and pre-hooks on the unmodified model, round index = call count of core[0] within a run. Arms apply at rounds >= 9 only (loop index 8 is the ninth iteration): S-zero subtracts step_emb[7] from the block input; S-mean then adds the mean of rows 0-7; S-reset uses ts = t mod 8 for a second look of 8 more rounds with no program writes (Rs and vals unchanged) and compares the two answers; M-hold rescales each token's output to its round-8 per-row RMS; drift-off subtracts a per-round calibration mean of block edits taken from 512 disjoint rows; NOOP-freeze index uses ts_i = min(t, t*_i) per row. Report L=0 and L>=1 separately; loops:8 output must be bit-identical to unedited. Params 0. (A scratch-copy one-liner for S-zero is Z = Z + (step_emb[ts] if t < n_loops else 0) at ledger.py:312.)
idea.why: The 16-round drop is -1.46 in-dist on average over six confirm seeds and sits in no-program rows (L=0 -1.87 and -1.45; L>=1 -0.11 and 0.00). One step addition is small (init norm about 0.32 against a state norm of about 130 at round 1, trained norm not measured), and the norm increments pass the clamp boundary smoothly (4.39 then 4.47 on seed 100; 9 rounds gives +0.02 and -0.04 in-dist), so the repeated add is probably not the main cause. The probe separates it from magnitude and drift for the cost of six forward passes, and decides whether trained stability fixes (idea 18) are needed at all.

Rule 4 is breached in the falsifier. The 'proved wrong' sentence is decided on seeds 100 and 101 only, while the idea's own rules_check calls two checkpoints a screen. No noise floor and no sham control. The 0.2-point band is about 14 of 6,800 rows at its tightest, and no arm reports how many rows flip. Any perturbation at rounds 9 and later flips some rows, so the test cannot separate clock content from any change. A norm-matched random direction (norm about 3.8, same at each round 8 and later) is needed. M-hold's 'not the cause' mark (-0.8 or worse) is already met at baseline on seed 101 (-0.85, PROBE.json M1), so that falsifier is satisfied trivially.

The NOOP-freeze arm cannot pass its own mark. ts_i = min(t, t*_i) changes the clock only on rows with a program. L>=1 rows lose only -0.11 and 0.00 (PROBE.json M1 by_len), while the mark requires closure from L=0 rows, which this arm leaves unchanged as written. No-program rows have no t*_i (L=0 is 4,007 of 6,800 rows, shown). If t*_i is the gold program length, the arm is an oracle. It must be the model's own predicted NOOP onset (argmax of p(NOOP) per round from control 0, ledger.py:323-326), and the arm should say it moves program rows only, or be dropped.

The run count and row sets are inconsistent. 'Six forward passes' conflicts with seven arms (Baseline, S-zero, S-mean, S-reset, M-hold, drift-off, NOOP-freeze) at loops 8 and 16 on two seeds, which is about 28 runs over 6,800 rows before any split. The pass marks also mix the 6,800-row probe (-1.15, -0.85) with the 1,360-row RESULT set (-1.62, -1.76); one row set must be named. The 0.5 h estimate is untested.

The mechanism is framed loosely. The heads apply LayerNorm to the controller (ln_z at ledger.py:321 and 342), so a global rescale of the vector cannot change any head output. M-hold changes answers only through the relative size of later block updates (residual adds at ledger.py:121, 123, 124). S-zero changes direction by about 3% per round. The arms should be labelled by the mechanism each tests: clock content, relative update size, or common-mode drift.

The decision this informs is not stated. The clamp exists only where rounds exceed the step table: current 8-round B2, and any design past 8 rounds (H1 with cap 32, where the choice is between adding learned step rows and stopping the clock). The 8a rung uses 12 rounds with a 12-row table (per the brief's 8A-SPEC addendum G), so a null on B2 would not transfer to it. The idea should name the decision it informs.

S-reset's 'second look' is not an independent check. It is a 16-round answer on the same trajectory, so its agreement with the 8-round answer is correlated. This overlaps the answer-unchanged-for-k stop already listed as suggested in the code notes (probe_hooks). The 0.95 agreement mark has no base rate; in_dist accuracy at 8 rounds is 89.4 and 90.5 (PROBE.json M1).

Implementation traps for the hooks. The round index is a call counter on core[0], but nothing resets it at the start of each run(), so a global counter across batches would edit the wrong rounds. S-reset needs step_emb[7] removed and step_emb[t mod 8] added inside the hook, and that edit point (ledger.py:312) is not specified. The 512-row calibration source for drift-off is not stated; it must be dev rows disjoint from the probe set.

Rule check. S-mean (mean of rows 0-7, norm about 1.0-1.2, shown) and drift-off (512-row calibration mean) are dataset-derived constants, acceptable only as probe-only and not for deployment; the idea says so for drift-off but not for S-mean. A zero-parameter clock change, if adopted, is a model rule the model runs itself, but it does not let the model choose its round count, so it does not advance Ben's key rule (rule 10) by itself.

The round-1 state (about 130) is the wrong comparison.

The clamp-boundary smoothness is not evidence. ts = min(t, n_loops-1) (ledger.py:308) gives row 7 at iteration index 7 and again at index 8, so the added vector does not change at the boundary. The two increments compared (4.39 then 4.48 on s100, PROBE M5) both contain the row-7 add. The increment series still rises through round 8 (1.37, 2.70, 3.28, 3.95, 4.13, 4.28, 4.39) and plateaus near 4.6 from round 13, so no kink is expected whatever the cause. Remove this from the 'why' (shown: results/40-loops-probe/PROBE.json).

The L=0 versus L>=1 split cannot test the add. The add is one vector for every row (ledger.py:312), so it reaches both row types by the same path; a row-type difference reflects readout sensitivity, not cause. The program-row side is nearly empty: the L>=1 gap is -0.11 on s100 and 0.00 on s101, and the s100 value is 3 net rows of 2,793 (3-step family: -0.67 on 447 rows). The NOOP-freeze arm breaks its own identity gate. ts_i = min(t, t*_i) changes the embedding at rounds 4 to 7 of an 8-round run for any row with t*_i < 7, so loops:8 output is not bit-identical as the pass mark requires. t*_i is also undefined: if it is the gold program length it leaks gold into a forward pass; if it is the model's own NOOP onset it is a per-row index, a different question from the earlier freeze test (reported at -3.4 and -5.7 in the area summary, not re-checked here). The name says freeze, but the arm only changes an index. Drop it or redefine it (shown by arithmetic on the arm text against ledger.py:308).

S-mean is ambiguous and confounds size with direction. 'Adds the mean of rows 0-7' does not say whether row 7 is replaced or the mean is added on top. The mean's norm (about 1.2 on s100) differs from row 7 (3.1), so it is not a magnitude control. A norm-matched random-direction control (S-rand: a fixed random vector with row 7's norm, added at rounds >= 9) is needed. Without it, a null on S-zero cannot say whether size or the trained direction matters.

Closure is reachable trivially. Freezing the state after round 8 reproduces the loops:8 answer exactly (same code path, same readout), so any arm that stops the state moving closes the gap by construction. M-hold (a magnitude clamp) can do this in part. Each closure claim needs the freeze-at-8 ceiling (free, since it equals the loops:8 answer) and the per-round RMS of the arm's state, which must still grow. Otherwise a closure does not identify the step add.

The decision bands leave gaps and are inconsistent. Closure: gap >= -0.3 on both seeds (needs +0.85 on s100 and +0.55 on s101, about 58 and 37 net rows of 6,800). Not-the-cause for S-zero and S-mean: within 0.2 of baseline (-1.15 and -0.85). Not-the-cause for M-hold: -0.8 or worse, which is one-sided, and the s101 baseline (-0.85) already meets it. Partial reductions (for example -0.6 on s101) fall in no category, and partial is the most likely hard outcome. Define a partial band and apply one rule to every arm (shown: arithmetic on the idea's pass_mark text).

The 0.2 band has no noise estimate. The probe is deterministic, so 'pass by chance' concerns row sampling, not run-to-run noise. The baseline gap moves with the row set: s100 is -1.15 on the 6,800-row probe and -1.62 on the 1,360-row RESULT set (results/29-b2-screen/B2_s100/RESULT.json); s101 is -0.85 and -1.76. 0.2 points is about 14 net rows of 6,800. probe_loops.py writes only aggregates (percent by K, M1 to M5, gates) and does not save per-row hits (shown: probe_loops.py json.dump at the end of main), so arm-minus-baseline flip counts and a paired CI cannot be recomputed. Save per-row hits for every arm and report rows changed and a paired bootstrap CI.

Rule 4 conflict. Two screen checkpoints can pass a screen or fail one; they cannot prove 'wrong'. The idea's 'proved_wrong' should read 'fails screen' unless six seeds are used. The six confirm checkpoints are present (scratchpad b2ckpt/B2_s200 to B2_s205, each with a .sha256 file), so a six-seed run costs about three times the screen and is the first thing that could support a claim.

Cost is misstated and unmeasured. rules_check says 'six forward passes'. The arm list gives 6 arms x {8, 16} rounds x 2 checkpoints = 24 full passes, plus chain-5 and the 512-row calibration pass. In round-units (6,800 rows x rounds), the D6 set is about 165 per checkpoint against 136 for the PROBE M1 sweep, so about 1.2 times the PROBE run. probe.log and design/LOOPS-probe.md contain no run times, so the 0.5 h figure is untested. No GPU is needed; 3.3M params of inference is far under 16 GB on the PC or the M1 Mac. The dev rows are not in project files, so the probe cannot run here (untested).

Round counting by hook is fragile. No hook fires at the start of run(), so a round index based on the call count of core[0] must be reset per batch. The repo's pattern is a lesion argument inside ledger.run() (ctl27 at ledger.py:315-316, with the lesion list in the Ledger LESIONS attribute). A run()-level lesion at line 312 is 2 to 3 lines, reads t directly, and makes the identity gate simple to check. A pre-hook on core[0] would see Z after the add (line 312 precedes the block loop), so subtraction is possible but brittle.

Decision value sits in the surprise branch. The norm arithmetic predicts a small S-zero effect (suggested, not measured). A null would leave the drift in trained block weights, so idea 18 would still be needed; the write-up should say so, so a null is not read as a fix. The idea's 'prior is low' is right, but the stated reason (init norm) is not.

Scope creep. NOOP-freeze, M-hold and drift-off measure magnitude and drift. drift-off is a fitted per-round correction (a calibration mean) and is not deployable; M-hold uses the round-8 state of each row. These belong to the idea 18 test, where a deployable form would be more step_emb rows or a norm rule the model runs itself (suggested).
critiques.rescue: Keep the probe but shrink it and fix the marks. (a) Zero compute, already done in this review: put the trained row norms (3.14 to 4.13 across the eight checkpoints) and the per-round share (about 4 to 6 percent of one round's increment) into the idea in place of the init-norm argument. (b) Primary arms on all six confirm checkpoints (B2_s200-205, sha256-checked) plus the two screen checkpoints, as a run()-level lesion that touches rounds >= 9 only: S-zero, and S-rand (a fixed random vector with row 7's norm). Keep the loops:8 identity gate. Freeze-at-8 is reported as the ceiling; it costs nothing because it equals the loops:8 answer. (c) Save per-row hits for every arm and the 16-round baseline. Report rows changed, net gap, and a paired bootstrap 95 percent CI for arm minus baseline, on in_dist, split into L=0 and L>=1, plus chain-5. (d) Fixed marks: closure = CI excludes 0 and the arm recovers at least half of the baseline 16-minus-8 drop on every seed; null = CI within 0.2 points of 0 on every seed; partial = anything else, reported, not decided. (e) Move NOOP-freeze, M-hold and drift-off to the idea 18 test. (f) Cost about 290 round-units (2 arms x 24 x 6 checkpoints), close to one PROBE-sized sweep. Run on Ben's PC on CPU; no GPU. Proceed to idea 18 only if both arms are null or partial. chair.reasons:
CUT as a standalone test. It breaks no rule (CPU only, 0 params, dev rows only, diagnostic), but it is the weakest kind of cheap test: the likely answer is already in hand, and a null would change nothing Ben builds.

1. The cause is mostly excluded by evidence already in the project. (a) Shown: the register-loop arm A has no step embedding and no round index. I read register_loop.py:71-84, where rounds() adds only S + P and applies ln_s each round. A still drops at 2x its trained rounds: 84.12 to 82.35 on seed 100 and 84.63 to 83.16 on seed 101, which is -1.77 and -1.47 (results/20-screen-s100-w1/A_s100, results/22-screen-s101-w1/A_s101, RESULT.json, loops:12 vs final_eval; A trains 6 rounds). The idea cites A as a supporting arm but misses that A cannot have the ledger.py:308/312 clamp. (b) Shown: Test LR keeps the clamp unchanged and still cuts the B2 16-minus-8 drop from -1.62 and -1.76 (results/29-b2-screen B2_s100 and B2_s101) to -0.51 and -0.22 (results/37-pc-loop-readout LR_s200 and LR_s201). So the drop tracks what the heads were trained to read, not the step index. (c) Shown: the 9-round null (+0.02 and -0.04, PROBE.json M1) fits a small clamp effect but is also what any cause would give at one round, so it does not separate them. The idea's 'smooth norm increment at the boundary' is not evidence either, because row 7 is already added at loop index 7, so the added vector does not change at the clamp (ledger.py:308, 312).

2. The size argument in the idea is stale, and the corrected one gives a lower prior. The idea uses the init norm 0.32. Three critics read the trained step_emb row 7 from the checkpoints and agree on 3.1 to 4.1 (B2_s100 3.14, B2_s101 3.43, confirm seeds 3.36 to 4.13). I did not re-read the weights. Against a per-round controller edit of about 70 in norm (M5 RMS increments of about 4.4 times 16), one add is about 4 to 6 percent of a round's change and under 1 percent of the round-8 state. The L split cuts the same way (suggested): the add is identical for L=0 and L>=1 rows (ledger.py:307-312), so it cannot explain a drop that exists only in L=0 (-1.87 and -1.45) and is flat in L>=1 (-0.11 and 0.00). That points to readout sensitivity and drift, not a clock. My prior that the clamp is the main cause is about 5 percent (suggested, below the idea's stated 'low').

3. The decision value is small. At deploy the thinker runs a fixed 8 rounds, so rounds 9 and later are never used. If H1 (cap 32) is built, it trains through rounds past 8 with per-round supervision, so the clamp is learned around and an untrained-model probe does not transfer to it. A null sends the budget to trained fixes, but Test LR and the A control already point there. A surprise closure would give a zero-parameter rule that still does nothing at deploy without a stop. Rule 10 is untouched: diagnostic only, the stop decision stays unsolved here as in H1.

4. The test as written has defects that would need rewriting. Rule 4: 'proved wrong' rests on two screen seeds; the six confirm checkpoints exist, but a six-seed run is about 3x the cost. No flip-noise control: 0.2 points is about 14 rows of 6,800, and a norm-matched random push is needed. The M-hold 'not the cause' mark (-0.8 or worse) is already met by the seed-101 baseline (-0.85). NOOP-freeze breaks the identity gate if it touches rounds under 9, has no t* for 4,007 no-program rows, and is an oracle if t* is the gold length. S-mean is ambiguous (replace or add). S-reset is off-distribution. The pass marks mix the 6,800-row probe (-1.15, -0.85) with the 1,360-row RESULT set (-1.62, -1.76). 'Six forward passes' is really about 24 to 28 passes per checkpoint. probe_loops.py saves only aggregates, so flipped-row counts cannot be recomputed. The dev rows are not in project files, so it runs only on Ben's PC. The one-line cost estimate (0.5 h) is untested.

5. Only salvage worth keeping: if the idea-1 loop probe (probe_loops.py on the same checkpoints and rows) is already being run on Ben's PC, two extra arms cost almost nothing. See plan_guidance. Otherwise do not schedule it.
chair.revised_idea: Do not run D6 as its own test. If the loop probe (idea 1) is run anyway, add two arms to it as free extras, with no separate ranking. Arm S-zero: an in-run() lesion in the style of ctl27 (ledger.py:315-316) that skips the step_emb add when t >= n_loops, for the Z add at line 312 only. Arm S-rand: a fixed random vector with row 7's norm added at the same rounds, as the flip-noise control. Use the six confirm checkpoints plus the two screen ones, one machine, one row set, a re-run baseline, per-row hits saved. Report rows changed, the 16-minus-8 gap split L=0 and L>=1, and a paired bootstrap CI. Word the outcome as 'supports' or 'does not support', never 'proved wrong', unless all six seeds agree. Drop NOOP-freeze, M-hold, drift-off, S-mean and S-reset (the first three belong to the trained-stability test, idea 18, if it is ever run).
chair.plan_guidance: Only relevant if the two free arms are piggybacked on idea 1's probe. (1) Fix pass marks before running, same rule for every arm. The clock counts as a cause only if S-zero recovers at least half of the baseline 16-minus-8 drop on every seed and does more than S-rand. A null is a paired CI that includes 0 and stays within 0.2 points of the re-run baseline. Anything between those is reported as partial, not decided. (2) Round counting: loop index 8 is the ninth iteration; apply only at t >= 8; loops:8 output must be bit-identical to the unedited model on the same machine, and run the unedited baseline twice to prove the gate can pass at all (cross-machine same-seed values differ: 0.00 vs 1.40 and 10.81 vs 4.34 on the leak). (3) Implement as a lesion argument inside run(), not as a forward hook on core[0], so the round index resets per batch. (4) Use one row set and machine, and re-run the baseline; the 6,800-row gaps (-1.15, -0.85) and the 1,360-row gaps (-1.62, -1.76) differ by 0.5 to 0.9, more than the 0.2 band. (5) Name the decision: whether H1's cap-32 design needs learned step rows past 8; do not read a null as a fix, since the drift is then in the trained block weights, and the shown fix is per-round answer loss (Test LR, 2 seeds, failed stability and leak marks on seed 200 only). (6) Keep the labels: row-7 trained norms 3.1 to 4.1 are shown by three critics' reads, not re-read here; the A-arm control (no step embedding, -1.77 and -1.47 at 12 vs 6 rounds) is shown in RESULT.json and register_loop.py; the clamp prior of about 5 percent is suggested; everything about what S-zero would do is untested. (7) Plain-language note for Ben: extra thinking rounds hurt a little even in a model that has no round counter at all, so the repeated round-counter nudge is very unlikely to be the reason, and this test would mostly confirm that.

idea.title: Audit which crafting questions B2's language can write
idea.summary: Generate 8-, 10- and 12-item crafting worlds with count, yes/no and name questions, and run the real parser plus the reference search to count which fit B2's limits (9-entry op head, 7 steps, 16 prompt numbers, 208-character prompt, 8-character answer, exact division). No model, no GPU. Report every cell at the caps 7, 11 and 16, because the cap lift is planned.
idea.change: New CPU generator and audit script beside rules_real.py (for example creative/craftworld.py and audit_craft.py). Each row goes through progparse.to_program/program_for and rules_real.reference (BFS). Recipes 'a + b -> c' or '2 a -> c', goal depth 1-4, item names 3-8 letters, 200 questions per cell. Name-answer questions are reported separately (WORD keys are content-free, so they need the copy path). Hand-counted expected failures: dovu count 8 steps, receipt inverse 9, two-gather trip about 15, helo 11. Params 0.
idea.why: Every crafting stepping stone (dose tests, plain-decoder worlds, T1 tools) assumes its questions fit B2's language, and nothing has measured that. C2 kinds were kept only when a reference program fit 7 steps, and the P0 probe already found kinds B2 cannot write (dates, string edits). A recipe table with counts is likely to exceed 16 numbers or 208 characters, which would be the first concrete reason to prefer an outside tool that reads recipes.

evidence.claim: Caps: N_RES 7, N_NUM 16, W_MAX 64, op set NOOP plus 8 ops, MAX_PROMPT 208, MAX_ANS 8; rows over 7 steps get no program target (528 train rows, all list_stats).
evidence.label: shown

evidence.claim: C2 kinds were kept only if a reference program fit B2's executor within 7 steps (BFS, 600k-state budget).
evidence.label: shown

evidence.claim: No crafting-world generator or recipe code exists in creative/ or reader/custom_io; C5 'needs plan ops from B2's owner'.
evidence.label: shown
evidence.source: grep of code folders; creative-roadmap-2026-10-06.md line 224

evidence.claim: P0 found held-out kinds B2's language cannot write (dates, string edits).
evidence.label: shown

evidence.claim: Hand step counts (dovu 8, receipt inverse 9, two-gather about 15, helo 11) are exact.
evidence.label: untested

test.where: Any CPU (M1 Pro or PC); generator and checker only; no model, no GPU.
test.arms: World size 8/10/12 items x question type (count, yes/no; name reported apart) x goal depth 1-4 x cap {7, 11, 16}; 200 questions per cell.
test.pass_mark: At least 90% of 8-item count and yes/no questions at depth 1-3 have a reference within 7 steps and 16 numbers; at least 95% of all prompts fit 208 characters; the failing set matches the hand counts. Depth 4, 10/12-item shares and the 11/16-cap columns are reported without a mark.
test.proved_wrong: Under 60% representable at depth 1-3 for 8-item worlds (the op set, not learning, blocks C5 on B2; first stone becomes the outside tool), or under 80% of 12-item prompts fit 208 characters, or the failing set differs from the hand counts (recount before building anything).

idea.rules_check: R1 test tool only. R2 exact search, no teacher. R4 CPU audit claims nothing needing seeds; marks fixed here. R5 check generated prompts against protected-panel hashes before any later use. R6 CPU. R7 over-long rows are dropped and counted, never cut. R9 no village code. R10 not a deploy step.
idea.closest_prior: rules_real.py representability search (C2 kinds) and progparse.coverage; neither covers crafting goals or the prompt, number and answer caps.
idea.autonomy: Measurement before training; nothing runs at deploy. It must not become a deploy-time filter that decides which questions the model may answer.
idea.director_note: Check that step counts come from the real progparse parser, not hand counts, and that recipe tables with counts do not silently exceed the 16-number cap (likely for 10 recipes). Check the cap columns match the planned K1/8A addendum E lift, so the result is not stale after the cap changes.
idea.note: Check that step counts come from the real progparse parser, not hand counts, and that recipe tables with counts do not silently exceed the 16-number cap (likely for 10 recipes). Check the cap columns match the planned K1/8A addendum E lift, so the result is not stale after the cap changes.

problems: Does not measure C5's blocker. C5 asks for plans (sequences of crafting actions) and its own row says 'Needs plan ops from B2's owner' (creative-roadmap-2026-10-06.md:224, shown). The 9-entry op head (NOOP plus 8 arithmetic ops, progparse.py:11, shown) cannot express craft or gather actions at all. The audit scores count, yes/no and name answers over a recipe table, so a pass would not show C5 is feasible. The idea's own proved-wrong branch already concedes the op set blocks C5, so the audit has little decision value for C5.

The 'reuse rules_real.reference' claim is false as written (shown). rules_real.reference(kind, params) builds its row from fn(kind, params) (rules_real.py:73-85), so it cannot take a crafting row. fewshot.find_reference reads only fewshot-format prompts through fewshot.parse, which expects x -> y pairs plus one query (fewshot.py:25, 236-243), and it requires an integer answer (int(row['answer'])). Name answers cannot go through it. A new multi-input search is needed. Budgets also differ: rules_real passes 600k states (rules_real.py:80, 109), while the fewshot default is 200k (fewshot.py:235).

The progparse check is circular and weaker than a true reachability test (shown). to_program accepts only fixed arithmetic step shapes (progparse.py:117-161), program_for needs family, answer and steps fields (progparse.py:175-182), and operands are matched by value only (progparse.py:40-41). A generator must therefore write steps in the parser's grammar, so a parse pass tests the generator's own writing, not whether B2's executor can find the program. Use an executor search as the reachability test, and keep progparse only as a generator self-check.

The cap columns do not match the planned caps. (a) N_RES=7 is tied to the loop count: writes happen only when 1 <= t <= N_RES (ledger.py:319) with n_loops=8 (ledger.py:11-12, shown). A 16-step program therefore needs at least 17 rounds, so the 11 and 16 columns are model changes, not parser constants. Extra test-time rounds already cost -1.9 and -1.6 pooled-5 (redesign-ideas-2026-10-07.md:148, shown there). (b) The planned lift is data-sized: 8A-SPEC section 15, E1, sets each B2 cap to the longest training case (8A-SPEC-2026-10-07.md:308-317), and K1 lifts to 16 only for T1 (PLAN-AND-MARKS-2026-10-07.md:58, 70). The 11/16 values are not planned. (c) The 208-character cap is superseded for 8a: E2 moves cloze chunks up to 280 letters (8A-SPEC section 15). The audit should report 208 and 280 as separate columns.

The hand-counted example failures are unanchored (shown). The names dovu, helo, 'receipt inverse' and 'two-gather trip' appear in no roadmap, design or creative file. The only hits are in reader/artifacts transcripts and a data tgz, which are unrelated. The mark 'the failing set matches the hand counts' cannot be checked as written. Either the example worlds must be written out in full before generation, or the mark must go.

The pass marks have undecided bands. The pass is at least 90% of 8-item count and yes/no questions at depth 1-3, and the kill is under 60%, so 60-90% has no decision. For 12-item prompts the kill is under 80% within 208 characters, and the all-prompt pass is 95%, so 80-95% is undecided. 'Depth' is undefined (goal depth of what?). The 'count' question type is undefined, since it needs a plan to count over.

Name questions are excluded from the marks, but C5's pass is about reaching items it never saw a plan for (creative-roadmap:224, shown), so names are the outcome that matters. Name answers can be checked exactly: a name is representable by WORD copy if it is a prompt word within the first W_MAX=64 words (progparse.py:8, shown). Give names a mark.

Rule 7 and addendum E conflict. The idea drops prompts over the cap ('dropped and counted') and accepts a 95% pass, which lets the longest, hardest rows leave the set. Addendum E says caps fit the data, never the other way round (8A-SPEC section 15, E1). The audit should drop nothing and report the lengths the data needs.

Rule 10 risk. The audit is measurement-only now, but C6 already requires that practice kinds be 'checked first' for B2 expressibility (creative-roadmap-2026-10-06.md:230, shown). If a reference search is used to pick practice kinds, that is a researcher-side selection, which the autonomy rule forbids for anything that runs at deploy. Label the audit as a pre-ship measure only.

Stage 4 overlap is unaddressed. The whole-model roadmap's row 4 (whole-model-roadmap-2026-10-06.md:428, shown) names the crafting world as a customer of program-language growth and has a proposed mark. The idea's 'first stone becomes the outside tool' branch does not refer to that mark. The audit's result should feed row 4 rather than decide the tool path alone.

Grounding of the 'why'. 'Dose tests' is a visible-example curve in creative/design/v3/30-modes/sleep-research-round2-2026-09-25.md:39, not a crafting stepping stone. 'Plain-decoder worlds' is a baseline in 54-modes-and-demo-opus.md:57, not a world. No crafting or recipe code exists in creative/, reader/custom_io/ or learnlab/village (the only 'recipe' hits are training recipes), so the stones the why cites are not in the record.

Predicted failure not named. Exact-only DIV (progparse.py:26, ex) makes ceiling questions such as 'how many crafts for N items' cost several extra steps, so they are likely to fall outside 7 steps. The audit should split them out (suggested, untested).

Checked and correct (shown): N_RES 7, N_NUM 16, W_MAX 64, 9 ops (progparse.py:8, 11); MAX_PROMPT 208 and MAX_ANS 8 (data.py:11); the rules_real search uses 7 steps and 600k states (rules_real.py:80-86); two of P0's four kinds are not writable (creative-roadmap-2026-10-06.md:126); C5 row text (creative-roadmap:224). Params 0 and CPU-only are correct.
critiques.rescue: Rewrite as a measurement with fixed marks. (1) Crafting rows get explicit number slots, and reachability comes from a per-row executor search that reuses creative/programs.run and Try, with state merging as in fewshot.py:236-273. progparse is only a generator self-check. (2) Write the example worlds in full in the spec before generation, or drop the hand-count mark. (3) Split questions: arithmetic (count and yes/no, numeric answer, exact search within 7 steps and 16 numbers) and names (answer is a prompt word within the first 64 words, checked by WORD copy). (4) Report with no drops: max steps, numbers, words and characters needed by the generated set at 8, 10 and 12 items, and the share within 208 and within 280 characters. (5) Marks: pass if at least 90% of 8-item count and yes/no questions at depth 1-3 are within 7 steps and 16 numbers, and at least 90% of names are word-copyable. Kill if under 60% at 8 items, or under 80% of 12-item prompts within 280 characters. Anything between is revise, with the failing kinds named. (6) State up front that plan questions and depth 4 are out of scope, that C5's plan part is blocked on stage 4 ops, and that the output feeds whole-model roadmap row 4's mark. (7) Label the output measurement-only, with no use to choose practice kinds at deploy.
critiques.already_tried: Closest prior, verified: creative/creative/rules_real.py:80-101 (reference, C2 kinds, 7 steps, 600k states) and :109-120 (representable_params); creative/creative/fewshot.py:235-282 (find_reference and representability, fewshot-format rows only); code/reader/custom_io/models/progparse.py:168-223 (program_for and coverage, teacher step grammar). The audit would repeat the fewshot.representability idea on a new row type. No crafting-world generator, recipe table or cap-11/16 run exists in any file read.
critiques.expected_effect: A cheap CPU measurement (about 0.5 h, 0 params, no GPU, no training). It would show which crafting arithmetic and name questions the current executor could in principle express within the current 7-step, 16-number, 64-word and 208-character limits, and where those limits bind. It would not show whether B2 can learn those questions, can write plans for C5, or can use a 280-character prompt at its current size. Predicted, untested: 16 numbers bind first at 10 to 12 items, since recipe quantities add up; names are mostly representable by WORD copy; ceiling questions fall outside 7 steps.

problems: Autonomy walk-through, build-time steps (generator, parser, BFS reference, counting, choosing the rescue). All are hand code or researcher choices before shipping. Under rule 10's build clause this is allowed, and the idea runs nothing at deploy. This part passes.

Deploy step with no autonomous version: the shipped model deciding whether a crafting goal is inside its language. The only representability test the idea names (rules_real.reference, fewshot.find_reference) reads the answer key (fewshot.py:236 'reads the key') and runs a breadth-first search (fewshot.py:251-267) that the model cannot run at deploy. The idea says 'proved wrong' but gives no autonomous path. Candidate paths, all untested: an outside recipe-lookup or check tool the model writes a call to (rule 1 allows this), or a learned can't/stuck signal (C9 and H1 are spec only). Until one exists, the model cannot tell in-language goals from out-of-language ones.

Deploy perception step is hand-written: the world must be rendered into a prompt of at most 208 letters (data.py:11, 107) by environment code. That code chooses what the model sees and in what order, which sits between the world and the question. Suggested autonomous version: the model asks for state through a tool call (for example inventory() or recipe(item)), so it chooses what to look at. The idea does not mention this step.

Curriculum-selection risk: the 90% pass (8 items, depth 1-3) would, if used to choose which kinds or world sizes get trained, have a researcher fit the practice set to B2's limits. Hand-made pre-training data is allowed (rule 1, rule 10 build clause), but the result would then say nothing about the real game's recipe sets, which the audit does not include. Real game prompts may also be longer than the caps set from training data (8A-SPEC section 15, E1). Keep the audit report-only, and add the real game's recipe table as a separate row (suggested).

Blocking bug for the idea's own route: rules_real.reference cannot run on crafting prompts. fewshot.parse returns None unless the prompt is example pairs plus one query with at most 16 numbers (fewshot.py:24-31). find_reference then indexes None (fewshot.py:240-241) and crashes. Even on pair-shaped prompts the search seeds only the query slot and the four constants (fewshot.py:244-246), so recipe and inventory numbers are never operands. SEARCH_OPS also leaves out CMP (fewshot.py:232), which the executor and progparse both have (progparse.py:11, 30). As written, the audit would report most two-number recipe questions as not representable, which measures the search, not the language.

Two representability routes, with no rule for which one sets the pass mark. progparse.to_program accepts only the step-text forms written for the old families (progparse.py:117-161) and raises 'unparsed step' for anything else (progparse.py:162). So the parse route measures how the generator writes its steps. The BFS route shows existence within a budget. Budget misses are 'not shown representable', never 'unrepresentable' (rules_real.py module docstring; fewshot.py:237-238). The idea's 'under 60% representable ... proved wrong' reads budget misses as failures. With 10-16 numbers, each BFS depth tries every slot pair times 7 ops (fewshot.py:251-267), so a 600k-state budget (rules_real.py:80) would likely run out by depth 2 or 3 (suggested; computed from the code, not run).

The audit tests arithmetic answers, not plans. C5 (creative-roadmap-2026-10-06.md, C5 row, about line 224) needs the thinker to write world plans, with the simulator as checker. Count and yes/no questions test only whether a final number is a short arithmetic chain over the prompt numbers. Which recipe to apply, what to gather first and when to stop are not measured, so a 90% pass says nothing about C5's plan language. Add a plan cell whose gold is a sequence of world actions, checked by a simulator.

Caps are stale against the sealed plans. 8A-SPEC section 15 (E1, E2) and section 17 (G1, G2) set each cap to the longest training case: 11 program steps, 91 numbers, 208 words, 280 letters and answers up to 35 letters. PLAN-AND-MARKS line 70 (K1) lifts steps to 16 for T1. The idea's 16 is the current number cap (progparse.py:8), not the planned 91. Its 208-letter gate is stale (280), and its 8-letter answer cap is stale (35). The idea does not say whether 7/11/16 are steps or numbers. The audit needs separate axes: steps 7/11/16, numbers 16/91, letters 208/280, answer letters 8/35.

Silent truncation and misattributed failures: prompt_numbers keeps only the first 16 digit runs (progparse.py:18). When a gold step needs a number past that, Builder raises 'operand not found' (progparse.py:53), and program_for returns that as the reason (progparse.py:172-173). The audit would then label cap failures as missing operands. Count prompt digit runs, prompt letters and steps directly from the raw text, before any parsing.

Dropping rows before scoring inflates the pass rate. The idea's rules_check says over-long rows are 'dropped and counted'. If the percentage is taken after the drop, it is computed only on questions that already fit. The denominator must be the full generated set. The 8A plan rules out this kind of drop: G1 (8A-SPEC section 17) says a filter that drops rows a model's shape cannot hold is a cap, and E1 says caps fit the data. The drop must not be shared with any training build.

The hand counts cannot be traced. 'dovu', 'helo', 'receipt inverse' and 'two-gather' appear in no project spec. zgrep finds 'helo' (1,679 times) and 'dovu' (11 times) in /mnt/project-files/data-pool/built/web_slices_8a.tgz, as ordinary web words. That check is circular until the generator exists, so the counts should be recomputed and not used as a mark.

Verdict: plan, but only as a rewritten, low-priority, measurement-only cap report. As written the idea would not run, and its headline question has little decision value for the north star.

Checked by me in the files (shown):
- The reuse claim is false. rules_real.reference(kind, params) (rules_real.py:80-101) builds a canonical "Examples: x -> y ... Now q -> ?" row and calls fewshot.find_reference. That function calls fewshot.parse, which only accepts example pairs plus one query. It seeds only the query slot and the 4 constants. SEARCH_OPS leaves out CMP (fewshot.py:232), which yes/no answers need. A crafting prompt cannot go through it. A new multi-slot search is needed, so "no new search code" and the 0.5 h estimate are both wrong.
- fewshot.find_reference returns None for both "not found" and "budget hit" (fewshot.py:236-238, 268-269). Its docstring says None means "not shown representable", never "proved unrepresentable". The "proved wrong: under 60% representable" mark cannot be read from it as written. My own check of the loop found nothing that fixes this.
- The hand-count examples (dovu 8, receipt inverse 9, two-gather about 15, helo 11) are in no .md, .py, .json or .txt note under /mnt/project-files. The critics found only unrelated hits in tgz and transcript files. The mark "failing set matches the hand counts" cannot be checked, so drop it.
- Caps are stale. 8A-SPEC addendum G (section 17) sets prompts up to 280 letters, answers up to 35, 91 numbers, 208 words, 11 program steps and 12 rounds, and G1/E1 say caps fit the data with no skip filter. The idea's 208 letters and 8-letter answers are the old B2 constants. K1 (PLAN-AND-MARKS) is a separate 16-call case for T1. The idea's "11 and 16" mixes steps with numbers.

Why the value is low (suggested, partly shown):
- C5's blocker is plan ops (creative-roadmap row C5: "Needs plan ops from B2's owner"; shown). The op head is NOOP plus 8 arithmetic ops and cannot write craft or gather actions. The audit tests only count, yes/no and name questions over a static recipe table. A pass does not show C5 is feasible. The idea's own kill branch ("the op set blocks C5") is already known.
- Representable does not mean learnable. B2 scores 25.0 on table_lookup and 56.2 on list_index (shown, 6-seed fact check), and those families are expressible. So even a 90% pass predicts little about B2 learning crafting questions.
- The likely outcome is mostly forced (suggested, untested): ceiling or exact-DIV questions cost about 5 steps each and fall outside 7; 10-12 item prompts miss 208 letters and fit 280.

Why it is still worth a rewritten pass: it costs no GPU and no params. It produces a crafting-question generator with exact-executor-verified gold step traces, which any later stone needs (B2 inside, T1 outside, a plain baseline). It also reports numbers no file has yet: steps needed against the 8-round and 12-round budgets (extra test-time rounds already cost -1.9 pooled-5; shown in redesign-ideas), digits per number against T1's copy failure at 4+ digits (shown in T1-SCREEN-RESULT), and word-token counts against W_MAX 64 (current train max is 50; shown in LIMIT-COUNTS). Build cost is the generator, hours not 0.5 h (suggested).

Rules: R1 and R10 pass because it is build-time only. It must not become a filter that picks practice kinds or world sizes (G1/E1; C6 "checked first" would be a researcher-side selection). The deploy-time gap, the model knowing a goal is outside its language, belongs to C9/H1 and is untested.
chair.revised_idea:
Title: Crafting-question cap report (measurement only, CPU, no model, no GPU).

What it does: write a small generator of text crafting questions with a pinned spec. For every question the generator emits its natural worked trace in B2's step grammar. Run that trace in the exact executor (creative/programs.run) to confirm it gives the gold answer (self-check, must be 100%). Then count what each question needs, straight from the raw text and the trace, before any parsing or dropping.

Pinned spec (fix and seal before generating):
- World size 8, 10 or 12 items.
- Recipe format "k a + m b -> c", with k and m in 1-4. Run a second variant with no counts (each is 1), written without numbers.
- Raw items plus crafted items.
- Item names 3-8 letters.
- Goal depth 1-3 (depth 4 reported only).
- Question types: (A) count: raw units needed to make n of a goal, with exact-multiple and ceiling counts as separate cells; (B) yes/no: can I make n of a goal from this inventory, answered with CMP; (C) name: which item is the goal or missing, answered by a prompt word.
- 200 questions per cell, three generator seeds. The denominator is the full generated set; nothing is dropped.

Counts per question, from raw text and trace:
- Steps needed, as the generator's trace length (an upper bound on the minimal program).
- Prompt digit runs.
- Word tokens, using the real data.py word split.
- Prompt letters.
- Answer letters.
- Max digits in any number and any intermediate value (T1 copy risk).

Minimal-step search: on 20 questions per cell at depths 1-2, run a new multi-slot search over all prompt numbers and constants, with CMP included. Report found, not-found and budget-hit separately, at 600k and about 6M states. This shows how far the natural trace is from minimal. Budget misses are "not shown representable", never "unrepresentable".

Caps reported as separate columns:
- Current: 7 steps, 16 numbers, 64 words, 208 letters, 8 answer letters.
- Addendum G: 11 steps with 12 rounds, 91 numbers, 208 words, 280 letters, 35 answer letters.
- K1: 16 calls for T1.
Also report the needed 95th-percentile cap for each count.

Marks, fixed before running:
- PASS-A: at least 90% of 8-item count and yes/no questions at depth 1-3 have a verified trace within 7 steps, 16 numbers, 64 word tokens, 208 letters and 8 answer letters.
- PASS-B: at least 90% of name questions have a gold answer that is one prompt word within the first 64 word tokens.
- PASS-C: at least 95% of 8-item prompts fit 208 letters.
- Kill: under 60% on PASS-A at 8 items (the op set or caps, not learning, block the stepping stone; the first crafting stone becomes the outside tool plus plan ops, gated on the T1 re-screen). Also kill if under 80% of 12-item prompts fit 280 letters (not 208).
- Band 60-90% on PASS-A: revise the world format and name the failing cell and the cap that bound; no tool decision yet.
- Everything else (depth 4, 10/12-item shares, ceiling counts, the 11 and 16 columns) is reported with no mark.
- Drop the dovu/helo/receipt/two-gather hand-count mark (the examples are not in any note).

Scope lines to write into the spec:
- This audits numeric-answer programs and name copying only. Plan ops (craft and gather verbs, per-episode state) are the real C5 blocker and are not tested.
- The result feeds whole-model roadmap row 4 and the T1 contract design (cells, tape, round budget).
- A pass does not show B2 can learn these questions. B2 gets 25.0 on table_lookup, which is representable.
- The report is measurement-only and build-time. It must not select practice kinds, world sizes or rows (8A-SPEC G1/E1), and it is not a deploy-time gate. The model deciding that a goal is outside its language is C9/H1 and untested.
- Generated prompts are checked against protected-panel hashes before any later training use (R5).
chair.plan_guidance:
The test plan must get these right:

1. Do not reuse rules_real.reference or fewshot.find_reference as-is (shown: they parse only example-pair prompts, seed only the query slot and constants, and omit CMP). Plan a new multi-slot search, and say that the main marks use the generator's verified trace as an upper bound. The BFS is a side check on a small sample.

2. Fix the generator spec before running: items, recipe format with and without counts, depth, question types, name pool and seeds. Define "depth" and "count" explicitly. Separate exact-multiple counts from ceiling counts (exact-only DIV makes ceil about 5 steps; suggested, untested).

3. Count steps, numbers, words, letters and digits from the raw text and the trace, not from progparse. Progparse has a fixed step-shape grammar and truncates numbers at 16, so a parse pass only tests how the generator wrote its steps.

4. Keep every generated row in the denominator. Report the cap columns at current, Addendum G and K1 values, not at 7/11/16 alone.

5. Report found, not-found and budget-hit separately for any search.

6. Time 20 questions per cell before the full run and state the CPU-hour estimate.

7. Use three generator seeds or per-cell intervals. With n=200, one seed has a standard error of about 2 points at 90%.

8. Give the 60-90% band a verdict (revise the world and name the cell).

9. Label every claim shown, suggested or untested.

10. Write the scope limits (no plan ops, representable does not mean learnable) and the autonomy limit (measurement-only, never a practice-kind filter, never a deploy gate) into the sealed spec.

11. Priority: low to medium, since the outcome is partly forced. Run it only as a side task while the T1 re-screen, EGE confirm and 8A ladder use the GPU, and treat the reusable generator with verified traces as the main product. Keep the small card experiments (B2, C1/C2) separate from the village model (R9).

plan.title: Crafting-question cap audit (CPU, measurement only)
plan.ben_line: We write practice crafting puzzles from fixed rules, then measure how big each puzzle is and whether today's model has room to hold it. No model is trained, and the results do not choose which puzzles the model practises.
plan.question: Do pinned text crafting questions (8, 10 and 12 items) fit B2's current limits (7 writes, 16 numbers, 64 word tokens, 208 characters, 8 answer characters), and which limit binds first, when each row is counted from its own verified program and the generator is sealed before it runs?
plan.one_change: One CPU audit tool: a pinned crafting generator, a counter that reads each row's raw text and verified writes, and a small minimal-program search on 20 questions per cell. No model, no training, and no edit to any B2 or T1 code path.
arms: Items 8 (3 raw + 5 crafted), 10 (4 + 6), 12 (5 + 7). One recipe per crafted item, using two distinct earlier items. Each raw item has an inventory count, sealed in the spec. About 156 cells per seed (3 sizes x 2 formats x 2 wordings x 13 question-depth cells).
Recipe format F1 'k a + m b -> c' (k and m in 1-4) and F0 with no numbers ('a + b -> c'). Same name pool in both.

Two pinned wordings of the same content: W-punct (sentence periods, 'I have 7 wood.') and W-terse (semicolons, no sentence periods). Word tokens use data.py's split (shown: data.py:149), so periods, semicolons, plus signs, arrows and question marks all count.

Question types: (A) exact count, units of one named raw item needed for n goal (n 1-4), multiplication only, MARKED; (B) ceiling count, stacks of size s (2-5), 5 writes (shown by grid check here; minimality untested), NO MARK; (C) yes/no about ONE named raw item (count plus one CMP), MARKED; the all-items yes/no is a NO-MARK cell; (D) name, the answer is one prompt word, no arithmetic, copy check only.
Depth d = crafting levels from raw items to the goal (a goal made only from raw items is depth 1). Marked at depths 1-3; depth 4 reported only.

Cap columns: current (7 writes, 16 numbers, 64 word tokens, 208 characters, 8 answer characters); Addendum G (11 writes with 12 rounds, 91 numbers, 208 words, 280 characters, 35 answer characters; shown: 8A-SPEC section 17); K1 (16 writes, T1 only, precondition unmet). Each measure also gets its 95th percentile per cell.
Search side check: 20 questions per (size, format, type A or C, depth 1-2), shared by both wordings, at 600k and about 6M states; found, not-found and budget-hit reported separately.
plan.seeds: Three new generator seeds, sealed before generating (not model seeds 200-205). 200 questions per cell per seed; each row keeps its seed. Marks use the pooled 600 per cell; per-seed values and 95% intervals are reported. The pooled standard error at 90% is about 1.2 points (per seed about 2.1).
plan.machine: Any CPU with the repo's Python and a CPU build of torch. reader/custom_io/data.py imports numpy and torch at lines 3-4 (shown), and programs.py imports progparse, which imports data.py. Preferably the M1 Pro, so the PC CPU and GPU stay free for the queue (suggested). No GPU. Torch is not installed in this snapshot, so nothing here was run.
pass_marks: PASS-A (8 items; count A and single-item yes/no C; depth 1-3; pooled over the three seeds): on BOTH wordings, at least 90% of rows have a self-verified program with at most 7 writes, 16 numbers, 64 word tokens, 208 characters and 8 answer characters, all five at once.
PASS-B (8 items, name questions): on both wordings, at least 90% of gold names are one prompt word within the first 64 word tokens. This is a copy check only; it does not show the name is derivable.
PASS-C (8-item prompts): on both wordings, at least 95% have at most 208 characters. Reported; not a kill on its own.

KILL: on both wordings PASS-A is under 60% AND under 60% of the depth 1-2 search sample is found within 7 writes at about 6M states. Only then the verdict is that the caps or op set block the stepping stone; the first crafting stone then needs an outside tool plus plan ops, gated on the T1 re-screen.

TRACE-BOUND: on both wordings PASS-A is under 60% but at least 60% of the search sample is found within 7 writes. Verdict: the generator's written trace is longer than the minimal program. No tool decision.

UNREADABLE: the two wordings differ by more than 30 points on PASS-A, or the search and trace shares differ by more than 10 points at 8 items, depth 1-2. Report the table; make no verdict until the search is fixed.
BAND: any other case (for example PASS-A between 60 and 90 on either wording). Revise the world format; name the failing cell and the cap that bound. No tool decision.

Reported with no mark: 12-item prompts within 280 characters (a note for the 8a caps, not a stone kill), depth 3 alone, depth 4, 10- and 12-item shares, ceiling and all-items yes/no cells, the Addendum G and K1 columns, digit lengths, budget-hit shares and 95th percentiles.
plan.proved_wrong: The idea (current caps keep crafting questions out of B2's reach) is proved wrong if PASS-A holds on both wordings at 8 items AND at least 90% of the depth 1-2 search sample is found within 7 writes. Then the caps are not the blocker and C5 is blocked by plan ops alone. The measurement itself is shown unreadable, not wrong, if the search and trace shares differ by more than 10 points at 8 items or the two wordings differ by more than 30 points on PASS-A; those cases are reported, not decided.
plan.null_risk: Yes, and the risk is high, so the lasting value is the cap table, not the verdict. Suggested, from a hand template computed here (not the generator; nothing saved): at 8 items the number cap passes on about 100% of rows and at 10 items on about 0%. The 64-word cap passes 0% of 8-item prompts with punctuation and 100% without, and 0% at 10 items either way. The 208-character cap passes 0-13% of 8-item prompts with 3-8 letter names and 7-99% with 3-5 letter names, depending on wording. So PASS-A and PASS-C can be decided by wording and name length alone, and a terse 3-5 letter wording could pass with no change to B2. The two-wording rule and the UNREADABLE rule exist to catch this. Suggested, naive writer: the all-items yes/no is at most 7 writes on about 40% of depth-2 rows and about 5% of depth-3 rows, so putting it in PASS-A would fail on semantics; it is limited to one named raw item. Exact counts of one raw item fit 7 writes on about 92-100% of rows at depths 1-3, so the write cap is unlikely to bind there. PASS-B is nearly always true when the generator puts the name in the prompt, so it carries little information. Shown: LIMIT-COUNTS-2026-10-07.json puts the longest training prompt at 50 word tokens, so 8-item crafting prompts would be longer than any training row. Shown: the verdict would also move if the 64-word cap were replaced by 208 (Addendum G), so the KILL depends on which caps are sealed.
plan.autonomy: Build-time measurement only. Nothing here runs when the model is deployed, and no result may choose training kinds, world sizes or rows (rule 10; 8A-SPEC E1 and G1). The sealed spec is researcher-chosen, which the build clause allows; the trained model never sees these choices. The deploy-time crafting step, where the model decides a goal is outside its language and asks for world state through a tool call, is not built or tested here; it belongs to C9/H1 and a sealed recipe or inventory tool, both untested. Any outside tool must be a tool the model chooses to call by writing text (rule 1). The generator, counter and search are hand-written scoring and build tools, which rule 1 allows; no LLM writes any data (rule 2).
steps: 1. Seal the spec before generating: item splits; both formats; both wordings verbatim; name rule (3-8 lowercase letters, no digits, unique within a world); inventory line form; the four question types and their definitions; the depth definition; three generator seeds; the cap columns; every mark above; and the scope lines (numeric programs and name copying only; plan ops untested; representable is not learnable; measurement only, no filter, no kind choice). Record the file's hash.

2. Build the generator as a new file, creative/creative/craftworld.py. Each row carries (a) its program as executor writes (op, slot, slot) and (b) a text trace in B2's step grammar. Hand-written and seeded; no LLM; no GPU.

3. Self-checks, all required. (a) Run every row's writes through programs.py (apply or run) and match gold on 100% of rows. Count writes first and do not use Try.make, which silently keeps only the first 7 steps (shown: programs.py Try.make). (b) Run the text trace through progparse.program_for and report parse success; this tests the grammar only. (c) On the search sample, any row whose verified trace has at most 2 writes and is reported not-found is a search bug, fixed before any read-out.

4. Counter, as a new file creative/creative/audit_craft.py, on raw text and writes, with no drops: steps = executor writes (not text lines); numbers = runs of digits in the raw prompt (progparse.prompt_numbers keeps only 16, so do not use it); word tokens = len(data.word_spans(prompt)); characters = len(prompt) (shown: data.py:107 asserts len, so 'letters' in the spec means characters); answer characters = len(answer); max digits per operand and result; flag any value at or above 1e9 (programs.apply treats it as invalid).

5. Minimal-program search (new, in audit_craft.py) on 20 questions per cell at depths 1-2: multi-slot, over all prompt numbers and constants 1, 2, 10, 100; ops ADD SUB MUL DIV MOD MIN MAX CMP; values as state; zero-step answers handled; budget-hit reported separately at 600k and about 6M states. Do not reuse fewshot.find_reference (shown: it crashes on non-pair prompts, returns None on budget hit, and returns None when the answer already equals an input or constant) or rules_real.reference (shown: one-input C2 rules, 600k budget).

6. Timing: run 20 questions per cell first, record seconds and peak memory, and write the CPU-hour estimate into the owning thread's notes before the full run. If 6M states cannot finish in the time available, the KILL rule cannot be applied and the verdict stays at BAND.

7. Full run: three generator seeds, 200 per cell per seed, both wordings, every cell and depth 1-4. Output per-cell shares with intervals, per-measure 95th percentiles, the cap table at current, Addendum G and K1 values, and the marks. Label every number shown, suggested or untested.
8. Apply the sealed marks in code, unchanged. Hash each generated prompt and check it against protected-panel hashes before any later training use (rule 5; the hash merge is not yet done).

9. Write the cap table first, the verdict second, with the wording sensitivity beside both. Feed it to whole-model roadmap row 4 (whole-model-roadmap-2026-10-06.md line 428) and to the T1 contract design (cells, tape, round budget). Do not use it to choose kinds, world sizes or rows.
files_to_touch: creative/creative/craftworld.py (new): pinned generator, both wordings, seeds, writes self-check
creative/creative/audit_craft.py (new): cap counter, writes checker, minimal-program search, marks
creative/creative/results/craft-audit/ (new): cell tables, JSON, timing, marks
reader/custom_io/data.py (read only): word_spans and _WORD (line 149), MAX_PROMPT and MAX_ANS (line 11), length assert (about line 107)
reader/custom_io/models/progparse.py (read only): N_NUM, N_RES, W_MAX (line 8); program_for for the grammar check only
creative/creative/programs.py (read only): run and apply; do not use Try.make for counting
Do not edit creative/creative/fewshot.py or creative/creative/rules_real.py
plan.depends_on: No model, GPU or training dependency. Needs: the sealed spec (owning thread); the 8A Addendum G caps as reference (whole-model-roadmap/8A-SPEC-2026-10-07.md section 17, already sealed); protected-panel hashes merged before any later training use. The K1 16-write column is conditional: PLAN-AND-MARKS-2026-10-07.md line 70 lists 'T1 passed its 6-seed confirm' as the precondition, but architecture/T1-SCREEN-RESULT-2026-10-07.md shows S3 failing (operand copy 14% at 4 digits and 1% at 5; answer copy 59% and 1%) and no 6-seed run. Priority low to medium: a CPU side task while the GPU queue (q39, q40, 8A) runs. The C5 plan-op blocker (creative-roadmap-2026-10-06.md line 224) is outside this audit.
plan.confirm: The measurement analogue of the six-seed confirm: three more generator seeds (six in all), same cells, both wordings, same marks, with per-cell intervals. A PASS or KILL is stated as a claim only if it holds on all six seeds pooled and on at least five of six seeds individually (rule 4 treats the three-seed run as a screen until then). Separately and later, a model-side probe: the six raw B2 checkpoints (code/b2ckpt, seeds 200-205) run zero-shot on 100 generated in-language prompts each, on CPU. Expected near zero (suggested from P0's 0.6-1.2% greedy on held-out kinds, creative-roadmap-2026-10-06.md section 2; untested for these kinds). That is a different claim and is not one of this idea's marks.

issues: Superseded caps (shown: 8A-SPEC-2026-10-07.md sections 15-17, E1, F4, G): PASS-A, PASS-C and KILL use 208 characters, 8 answer characters, 7 writes, 16 numbers and 64 words. E1 sets every cap to the longest training case, F4 sets one shared set, and Addendum G sets 280 characters, 35 answer characters, 91 numbers, 208 words and 11 writes. Under E1 a cap that bites is raised, so 'the caps block the stepping stone' cannot be a kill. The verdict is measured against caps that are already replaced.

Pointer reach is treated as a fit cap (shown: progparse.py:18 and 204; ledger.py:207 and 209). Only the first 16 numbers get slots and only the first 64 words get pointers. The reader still reads all 208 characters. An answer is blocked only when the gold program's operands or the answer name fall outside those ranges. PASS-A counts the whole prompt, so a prompt whose needed name is word 12 fails even though it is solvable.

Causes are not separated (shown: ledger.py:319 and progparse.py:199). The 7-write limit is architectural (8 loops give 7 writes). The word and number limits are pointer ranges. PASS-A bundles all five terms, and the TRACE-BOUND, KILL and BAND branches cannot say which term bound. A word-limit failure can be reported as 'the generator trace is too long'.

The decisive verdict is set by the researcher's free choices, not by B2 (shown: the plan's own null_risk text). The plan reports that 208 characters pass 0-13 percent of 8-item prompts with 3-8 letter names and 7-99 percent with 3-5 letter names. Name length and framing text decide PASS-A. A terse short-name wording could pass with no change to B2, so a PASS would show the wording, not the model.

Wrong or unsupported number (suggested; counted here with the data.py _WORD regex on one sample set of lines in the spec's format): 3 inventory lines of 5 tokens, 5 recipe lines of 7 tokens and a 10-token question give 60 word tokens and 213 characters for 8 items. That passes the 64-word cap and misses the 208-character cap by 5. The null-risk claim that the 64-word cap passes 0 percent of 8-item prompts with punctuation is not supported; 8-item pass or fail turns on framing text and name length, which the spec does not pin. Ten items in the same format are about 72 tokens (suggested).

Training range (shown: PLAN-AND-MARKS-2026-10-07.md line 62 'train max 204' characters; LIMIT-COUNTS-2026-10-07.json max_words 50 and max_nums 11). The sample 8-item prompt at 213 characters is longer than any training prompt. Length generalization is the likelier real bottleneck, and the audit does not measure it. Fitting a cap is not learnability.

Mislabelled and possibly wrong count: the plan says '5 writes (shown by grid check here)' for the stack-ceiling type B. No file contains that check, so the number is untested. DIV is valid only when exact (shown: ledger.py:85; programs.py:41), so a ceiling needs a multi-step trick. A hand derivation (MOD, SUB, DIV, MIN(r,1), ADD, with constant 1) gives 5 writes (suggested). The spec should write the program down and label it untested.

Yes/no grammar (shown: progparse.py:175-176). The only yes/no family in training is verify_claim, which ends in one CMP against a claimed number. Only equality-type yes/no is therefore in training (suggested from the code). A 'has enough' (greater-or-equal) yes/no needs a mapping that is not in training, and the audit does not flag it.

Format F0 is not number-free (shown: the spec's own inventory rule). Inventory counts still appear, and F0 recipes carry no quantities, so type A ('units of one raw item needed for n goal') is ill-defined unless every recipe is 1:1. The spec must say which.

Search budget and memory (shown: fewshot.py:29, 241, 262 and 268; the counts are suggested). fewshot.find_reference is correctly not reused (parse returns None on non-pair prompts and line 241 then indexes it). The new search will likely copy its pattern: one dict copy per new state. Per state, 8 items give about 2,600-2,900 children (18-19 slots, 8 ops, ordered pairs), so depth 2 is about 5-6 million candidate states; 12 items exceed the 6M budget. Several GB of memory per run is a likely outcome. 'Found within 7 writes' at depth 2 therefore measures the budget, and the KILL rule merges budget hits with not-found.

Machine conflict (shown: creative-pilot/MAC-JOB-9.md and progress-board/data.json, the creative job 9 entry): job 9 has been training on the Mac's CPU since 4:36 AM ET and ends about 4 PM ET, and the Mac asks Ben before its sealed-test step. A multi-hour CPU audit on the M1 now would slow job 9. The plan does not mention this.

Pooling hides cells (shown: spec text). PASS-A pools formats, depths 1-3 and types A and C at 8 items across three seeds. A failing cell, such as 8-item F1 depth 3, can be averaged away. If any mark stays, it needs per-cell thresholds.

Likely no decision and narrow scope (shown: the BAND and UNREADABLE rules, and the wording and name-length sensitivity above). BAND covers every case except the two extremes. UNREADABLE fires when the two wordings differ by more than 30 points on PASS-A, which the name-length spread makes likely. PASS-A also covers only types A and single-item yes/no, so a PASS says little about type B, type D or crafting in general.

Rule 4 and step 9 (shown: the spec's steps 8 and 9): the verdict from three generator seeds goes into whole-model roadmap row 4 and the T1 design before any six-seed claim. Count-only seeds carry little sampling risk, but a PASS or KILL label would travel with the result. Report it as measurement only.

Unsupported inference (shown: the plan's own scope line 'representable is not learnable'): 'the caps are not the blocker and C5 is blocked by plan ops alone' does not follow from the audit. The audit measures numeric arithmetic and name copying only. Recipe lookup and goal choice are not measured.

Rule 10 and test-world leakage (shown: the brief's rule 10; the spec says no result may choose training kinds but does not ban training from the generator): the pinned crafting generator is a researcher-written world. If its rows feed training, or its longest case sets E1 caps, the test world enters the model as a hand-picked practice set. The generator must be labelled test-only.

Not blind (shown: the null_risk section reports template numbers 'computed here, nothing saved' before the spec is sealed): the name rule (3-8 letters) and both wordings were chosen with those outcomes in view. The marks are fixed, but the free choices were informed by results, which weakens the pre-registration.

Hours have no basis (suggested): 5 hours is plausible only if each search takes tens of seconds, and no timing exists. Step 6's timing gate has no fallback except BAND. Dropping the 6M-state search takes the largest cost off the critical path.

Hash merge not done (shown: the spec's step 8 and the brief): protected-panel hashes are not merged, so generated prompts cannot be checked when they are made. Keep generated rows out of any training-reachable path until the merge exists (rule 5).

Cheaper test that answers the decision (suggested): gold-program counts and reach come from the generator's own trace with no search. B2's real sensitivity to placement and length is measurable on CPU with the existing raw checkpoints in minutes to hours. That measures B2's answers, which the count table cannot.

Context note on the brief (shown: /mnt/project-files/architecture/T1-SCREEN-RESULT-2026-10-07.md header): the T1 screen ran at about 5:10 PM on two rented RTX 5090s, so the brief's 'q40 queued after q39' is stale. Rule 6 allows rented GPUs only when both home machines are full, and the snapshot does not show that condition.

Checked and correct (shown): data.py:11, 107, 109 and 149; progparse.py:8, 18, 199 and 204; ledger.py:207, 209 and 319; programs.py:24-25 (Try.make silently drops steps past 7); fewshot.py:241; LIMIT-COUNTS max_words 50, max_nums 11 and 528 rows over 7 writes; the Addendum G values; the T1 S3 failure; PLAN-AND-MARKS line 70 (the K1 precondition is unmet); creative-roadmap line 224 (C5 needs plan ops); whole-model-roadmap line 428 (row 4). Pooled standard errors are correct: sqrt(0.9 x 0.1 / 600) is about 1.2 points and sqrt(0.9 x 0.1 / 200) is about 2.1 points.

fixed_plan.title: B2 placement and length probe, with a side cap table
fixed_plan.ben_line: We check whether today's model still gets the answer right when the number or name it needs sits late in a long prompt, or when its prompt is longer than any it trained on. We also count how many generated crafting puzzles would break its limits, but that count alone decides nothing.
fixed_plan.question: With everything else fixed, does B2 keep its answer when the needed number is past its 16th number slot, when the prompt has 18 numbers instead of 11, when the needed name is past its 64th word, or when the prompt is 70 word tokens instead of 50?
fixed_plan.one_change: One change: where the needed number or name sits and how long the prompt is, in paired hand-written items on the six raw B2 checkpoints. No training, no search, no new caps. The crafting cap table is a side output with no marks.
arms: N-in: 11 numbers in total; the two needed numbers are numbers 1 and 2 (inside the training range).
N-count: 18 numbers in total; the needed numbers are still numbers 1 and 2 (count beyond training, but the needed numbers stay inside the 16 slots).
N-late: 18 numbers in total; the needed numbers are numbers 17 and 18 (past the 16 slots). Same needed values and answers as N-count; only the placement changes.

C-offset (control for N-late): the two needed numbers are numbers 1 and 2, preceded by hand-written digit-free filler of long words whose total length equals the text before the needed numbers in N-late. The character offset matches; the count of numbers does not.
W-in: about 50 word tokens; the needed name is word 5 (inside the training range).
W-long: about 70 word tokens; the needed name is word 5 (length beyond training, name inside the 64-word reach).
W-late: about 70 word tokens; the needed name is word 66 to 68 (past the 64-word reach). Same items as W-long; only the placement changes.
W-control (control for W-late): the name is about word 20, preceded by long words whose total length equals the text before the name in W-late. The character offset matches; the word reach holds.
fixed_plan.seeds: Six raw B2 checkpoints, seeds 200 to 205, from code/b2ckpt with their sha256 sidecars. 150 paired items per arm per seed. Within each contrast the needed values and answers are identical in both arms, and only placement or length changes. Answers are computed by hand code. The item seed is fixed and the item file is hashed before the run.
fixed_plan.machine: Ben's M1 Pro on CPU, started after creative job 9 ends (about 4 PM ET 10-07). Needs a torch CPU build, which is not in this snapshot, so nothing here was run. No GPU and no PC queue.
pass_marks: P0 precondition: N-in and W-in exact match at least 80 percent on each of the six seeds. If not, report that the probe cannot answer this question and stop.

P1 count: N-count is at least 15 points below N-in (paired, per seed) on at least 5 of 6 seeds, which means beyond-training count breaks B2. N-count within 5 points of N-in on at least 5 of 6 seeds means count holds.

P2 slot reach: N-late is at least 15 points below N-count on at least 5 of 6 seeds AND C-offset is not at least 5 points below N-in on at least 5 of 6 seeds, which means needed numbers past slot 16 break B2 (the cap binds). N-late within 5 points of N-count on at least 5 of 6 seeds means the 16-slot cap does not bind here.
P3 length: W-long is at least 15 points below W-in on at least 5 of 6 seeds, which means prompt length breaks B2. Within 5 points on at least 5 of 6 seeds means length holds.

P4 word reach: W-late is at least 15 points below W-long on at least 5 of 6 seeds AND W-control is not at least 5 points below W-in on at least 5 of 6 seeds, which means needed words past 64 break B2. W-late within 5 points of W-long on at least 5 of 6 seeds means the 64-word reach does not bind here.
Anything else (between 5 and 15 points, or fewer than 5 of 6 seeds on a step): unresolved, reported as unresolved, with no claim.

Side output, no mark: for 8, 10 and 12 items, both formats and both wordings, one generator seed, 600 questions per cell. Report gold writes, numbers, word tokens, characters, operand and answer reach, and the shares over the current caps and over Addendum G. No search and no verdict.
fixed_plan.proved_wrong: The claim that today's limits (7 writes, 16 numbers, 64 words, 208 characters) or training length would block 8-to-12-item crafting puzzles for this checkpoint is proved wrong if P1 to P4 all hold on at least 5 of 6 seeds (no drop of 5 points or more on the relevant contrast). The count table alone can never prove or disprove a block, because it counts questions and does not measure B2's answers.
fixed_plan.null_risk: Medium. The count step may break first, which says more about the training range than about caps; the controls separate placement, character offset and count only within these arms. Per-seed paired standard error is roughly 3-4 points (suggested: 150 items, discordance near 20 percent), so the 15-point threshold is about 4 standard errors. The result concerns the q33 3M checkpoint with its 16-slot and 64-word caps, not the Addendum G shape (91 numbers, 208 words), so a 'holds' result does not carry over to 8a. The hand-written question wording may itself be out of distribution, which is why P0 is a precondition.
fixed_plan.autonomy: Build-time measurement on existing checkpoints with hand-written test items. No training and no deployed step. No result may choose training kinds, caps, rows or the generator (rule 10; E1 and G1). Deploy-time choices, such as whether the model asks a tool for recipes or inventory, are not built or tested here.
steps: 1. Write the item template, the arms, the 5- and 15-point thresholds, P0 to P4 and the side-output rules into a file, and hash it before any item is generated. Fix all framing text in the template so no wording is chosen after seeing counts.

2. Write the hand item generator as a new file (no LLM, no protected-panel text). Compute each answer by hand code. Check each arm's needed-number and needed-word index with the regexes the code uses (progparse NUM_RE and data.py _WORD).
3. After creative job 9 ends, install a torch CPU build on the Mac. Check the six checkpoint sha256 sidecars and load each raw B2 checkpoint through models/__init__.py load_model.
4. Run all eight arms on six seeds, 150 paired items each. Record exact match per item.
5. Compute per-seed paired differences and 95 percent intervals for the four contrasts. Apply P0 to P4 exactly as written. Report unresolved cases as unresolved.
6. Side output: one generator seed, 600 questions per cell, gold trace only, no search. Report reach and cap shares against both the current caps and the Addendum G caps, with no marks.
7. Record the item hash. When the protected-panel hash merge exists, check the items against it before any later use (rule 5). Keep the items out of every training path.
8. Send the results to whole-model roadmap row 4 and the 8A caps reference as measurements only. Make no training choice from them.

final.why: Park. It breaks none of Ben's rules and uses no GPU, but the answer is mostly forced by arithmetic and wording, and the caps it tests are being replaced. Shown: progparse.py:8,18 gives 16 number slots, 7 steps and 64 pointable words, and LIMIT-COUNTS shows the longest training prompt is 11 numbers and 50 words. Addendum G (8A-SPEC section 17) and E1/G1 set 280 letters, 91 numbers, 208 words and 11 steps, and say caps rise to fit the data. So a "caps block it" kill cannot change any decision. Suggested: by pencil, a "k a + m b -> c" recipe table has about 2 numbers per recipe, so 8 items need about 14 numbers and 10 items about 17. Whether a prompt fits 208 characters or 64 word tokens turns on name length and wording, and the two Haiku passes disagree on the 64-word result for 8 items. The real C5 blocker (plan ops, per-episode state) is not tested by either plan. The Haiku "fixed plan" is a different idea, a probe of B2's behaviour with placement arms. Its slot-reach arms (P2, P4) are decided by code, not by the model, since numbers past 16 have no workspace slot and words past 64 cannot be pointed at. Its precondition (P0, at least 80% on hand-written items) will probably fail, because B2 gets 34.7% on the variant split and 0-4% on new kinds. It also probes the q33 shape that 8A replaces. The reusable part, a crafting generator whose traces are checked by the exact executor, is worth building later. Build it after the T1 re-screen and the crafting contract (verbs, state, tape, round budget) are fixed, and let the cap table come out as a free by-product with no marks.
final.ben_line: Counting whether crafting puzzles fit the model's current size limits is cheap, but the answer mostly depends on how we word the puzzles and those limits are about to change, so wait until the tool-call design for the crafting world is settled.
plan_fixes: Do not run the placement probe (the Haiku 'fixed plan') as written. P2 (numbers 17-18) and P4 (words 65+) are decided by code, not by B2: no workspace slot exists past number 16 (progparse.py:18, ledger.py:207) and no pointer past word 64 (W_MAX). Drop their marks, or restate them as a code confirmation with no mark.

P0 (at least 80% on hand-written N-in and W-in items) will likely fail. B2 is 34.7% on the variant split and 0-4% on new kinds, so a new hand-written wording is out of distribution. Build the arms from existing in-distribution families (list_stats, table_lookup, copy_word) by extending them. That needs the skills generator, which is not in this snapshot, so it must run where the generator lives (the PC copy).

The arms mix length with density. Fitting 70 word tokens or 18 numbers inside the 208-character assert forces short words and punctuation-heavy text, which differs from training. The character-offset controls (long filler words) add another shift. State this confound, or test length with the 280-letter shape instead.

The probe targets the q33 shape (8 rounds, 17 vectors, 27 slots), which Addendum G replaces (12 rounds, 91 numbers, 208 words, 280 letters). E1/G1 raise any cap that bites, so a 'cap binds' result cannot change a decision. Say so in the spec, or wait and probe the 8A shape once a checkpoint exists.

If the crafting cap table is built later, pin the spec before generating. Pin the wording, name pool and length, the inventory line form, and the definitions of depth and count. Separate exact-multiple counts from ceiling counts. Label the 5-write ceiling program untested. Say what the F0 (no-number) format means for count questions, since every recipe is then 1:1.
