problems: [shown by code reading, not run] At loops:0 the talker mode is the same for every row. ledger.py:304 builds Z from parameters only (ctrl.weight and the reader place embeddings, expanded over the batch). With zero rounds Z is never updated, so zf = ln_z(Z[:,1]) (ledger.py:342) and lmode = mode_head(zf) (ledger.py:344) do not depend on the question. talk() takes one mode per row from lmode (ledger.py:391), so a zero-round run applies one NUM, WORD or GEN policy to every row. T1's tool.py:149 and 195-196 have the same structure. The idea's claim that only copy attention and the word-key pointer see the question is wrong. The NUM answer pointer keys (ks_, built from S0 at ledger.py:295 and 343) do see the question, and the mode decision does not see it at all. A per-row class analysis misses this.

[suggested, from shown per-family counts and research/data.md answer types] The hit pattern fits one global word-copy policy better than per-row shortcuts. Seed 201: copy_word 35/40, prop_eval 30/40, object_track 7/40 (copy_word, object_track are W type and prop_eval is a two-label F type, research/data.md lines 8, 22, 25). Seed 101: copy_word 18, object_track 18, prop_eval 16, seq_cycle 9 (W, research/data.md line 18). The proved-wrong rule needs families with 'over 50+ rows', but dev in_dist has 40 rows per family (1,360 rows over 34 families). Only the 6,800-row big build has 200 per family, and the idea makes that build optional ('if available'). The family-level falsifier is unreachable on the dev in_dist the probe names.

[shown in research/data.md line 67, not recomputed here] The constant-floor frame passes almost any leak. That file gives train-majority floors per family with an in_dist mean of 16% (syllogism 68, group_induct 65, verify_claim 57, prop_eval 55). Every B2 and T1 seed reads 0 to 10.8 at loops:0 (RESULT.json; T1-SCREEN-RESULT-2026-10-07.md line 16). Pooled excess (hits minus floor) is therefore about -5 to -16 on every seed, so the '<= +2.0' clause holds by construction, and the '> +5.0' falsifier needs a leak above about 21%. The 16% comes from a 2026-10-05 note on a seed-1 build and must be recomputed on the sk200k train. The phrase 'best constant answer from train (scored on dev)' must mean a constant chosen from train frequencies only, never from dev scores.

[shown, idea text] Two different floors are used. The change block defines excess as zero-round hits minus a per-family train constant. The pass_mark uses 'pooled excess over the reachable-class floor' (chance for classes A, B and D from candidate counts). These give different verdicts. copy_word at 35/40 on seed 201 is far above any constant floor and far above chance over candidate words, so the two definitions read it differently. The idea must choose one before it runs.

[suggested, reasoned from the counts above] The 'chance-level' test checks the wrong property. 'Top string covers >= 80% of rows in half the families' tests whether the output is constant, not whether the hits are chance. A content-keyed word pointer that copies the right word (copy_word 35/40) fails that test, while a constant output that matches a two-label family (prop_eval, research/data.md line 25) can pass it. The verdict would fire on the wrong cases.

chair.reasons:
Plan, but only as a cut-down, report-only diagnostic. It costs no GPU time and nothing is trained. Mark 4 (loops:0 <= 5% on every seed) matters because it gates the T1 and B3 confirms. The fact check reproduced that mark 4 rejects an identical design 88-94% of the time (shown by the Haiku checker). The test critic's bootstrap over the eight B2 loops:0 values puts the pass rate for a six-seed run at about 6% (computed from the eight values in RESULT.json). The idea as written is not safe to run, for five reasons.

(1) The mechanism in the idea is wrong or incomplete (shown; I read /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-learner/25dd80f7-54e0-50c0-b0e0-f697e28becce/scratchpad/code/reader/custom_io/models/ledger.py). At loops=0 the thinker state Z is built only from parameters (ctrl.weight plus the reader place embeddings). So zf = ln_z(Z[:,1]) and lmode = mode_head(zf) are the same for every row, and each checkpoint has exactly one talker route (NUM, WORD or GEN) at zero rounds. The row enters only through the keys: the number-slot keys (S0, from the prompt's numbers), the word keys Kw (plus word_content), and the GEN copy keys over the reader output X. The query is constant and the keys vary by row.

(2) A per-row class split mostly measures which route a checkpoint uses. Class C (computed) cannot be hit on a NUM or WORD route by construction. A NUM answer is a prompt number or one of 4 constants, a WORD answer is a prompt word, and class C answers equal none of those (shown, from the progparse.py and ledger.py reading by two critics). So class C <= 2.0 passes by construction on those seeds. It tests anything only on a seed whose zero-round route is GEN.

(3) The falsifier cannot fire on the named data. Dev in_dist has 40 rows per family (shown: every by_family n is 40 in B2 RESULT.json lesions.loops:0.in_dist), and the clause needs families with 50+ rows. The 6,800-row big build is not in this snapshot, and its rule-5 protected-panel hash check is not on record.

(4) The pass marks are not fixed in advance and are not coherent. The 2.0 and 5.0 cutoffs and the 80%-top-string clause were written after the noexec floor (0.24-0.82) and the leak values were seen. The idea uses two different floors (the train constant and the chance floor over candidates) that give different verdicts. The "top string covers >= 80% of rows" test checks whether the output is constant, not whether it is chance. A word pointer that copies the right word (seed 201, copy_word 35/40) fails that test, while a constant output that matches a two-label family passes it. A train-majority floor of about 16% on in_dist (from an older, unrecomputed note, research/data.md line 67) would make "excess <= 5" true on every seed by construction.

(5) The restatement path breaks the rules. Restating mark 4 after reading the results loosens a sealed mark, which MARKS-D0-T1 forbids, and it needs Ben's explicit approval and 6 paired seeds (rule 4). T1 has only 2 checkpoints.

What survives:
- Shown: per-seed zero-round hits differ in kind. Seed 201 hits copy_word 35/40, prop_eval 30/40, story_chain3 12/40 and digits_parity 9/40. Seed 101 hits copy_word 18, object_track 18 and prop_eval 16. Seed 203 hits word_filter 22, letter_ops 12 and odd_one_out 11. Seed 204 hits odd_one_out 13 and list_index 8. Seeds 100, 200, 202 and 205 are 0.
- Suggested: this pattern fits one learned zero-round route per seed plus a constant query. That is why the pattern differs by seed, and it contradicts the old "word-pointer families only" story (REPORT item 4), which seeds 203 and 204 do not fit.
- The previous explanation was already retracted once (PASS-MARKS addendum 14), so a cheap histogram is worth having before anyone designs a fix or an amended mark.

The value is understanding what mark 4 measures. The cheap lever for the measurement area is separate from this probe. It is a wording fix and a choice of mark form (every-seed versus six-seed mean), which Ben must seal before any confirm. Rank this idea low to mid: cheap, informative, but it changes no verdict and does not speed up any experiment.

Rule check for the revised probe:
- Rule 1: measurement and scoring only.
- Rule 4: no claim made.
- Rule 5: dev in_dist only until the hash check passes.
- Rule 6: CPU only.
- Rule 9: B2 and T1 are both card line, reported separately.

Stage 0 also logs the route head's logit margin (top minus second) per checkpoint at zero rounds. Reading only: a near-tie flips the route on every row at once, so a route change between CPU fp32 and the stored CUDA bf16 run would show here.

Stage 1 prediction (from the code, shown: ledger.py lines 304, 342-344 and 391; tool.py run and talk): the head route is identical on all 1,360 rows of every checkpoint. Falsifier: any row whose head route differs from the rest (expected zero). The decoded route can differ from the head route only where talk() falls back to write-out (a word index past the row's word list, or a row with no words); those counts are reported, not judged.

Stage 2 reading, set now and descriptive (suggested, not a mark on any design): explained share = sum over families of max(hits of the family's most frequent zero-round output, hits of the family's train-majority answer), divided by all zero-round hits. At 50 percent or more, the fixed-guess reading is not falsified on that checkpoint; under 50 percent, its hits need a content-keyed explanation. The 50 percent line is a choice, and the raw counts sit beside it. Because the max takes the better of two guesses per family, the share is an upper bound on any one fixed guess per family, so under 50 percent is the informative result.

Stage 2 chance floor, reported beside every family and never in a verdict: expected hits if the route's pointer picked uniformly among its valid candidates (prompt numbers plus the constants 1, 2, 10, 100 on a number route; prompt words on a word route; write-out not computed). No per-family threshold: dev in_dist has 34 families of 40 rows (shown, RESULT.json by_family), so one row is 2.5 points.
plan.proved_wrong: The route idea is wrong on a checkpoint if (a) any row's head route differs from the others, which the code says cannot happen (shown: ledger.py run builds the controller state from parameters only at zero rounds, and tool.py does the same); or (b) its explained share is under 50 percent, which means its zero-round hits need a content-keyed explanation (a finding about that checkpoint, not a mark). The probe itself is wrong, and Stages 1 and 2 are void, if Stage 0 fails on any gate checkpoint. A class C hit (gold computed answer) on a number or word route is a coincidence (the computed value equals a prompt number, constant or word), so it is counted and reported, not used as a falsifier.
plan.null_risk: Stage 0 and the Stage 1 route prediction would pass with no real change, because they test the probe's wiring and the code reading; the route prediction is near 100 percent by construction, so passing it says nothing about the model. The Stage 2 reading depends on the 50 percent choice, so raw counts stay beside it. Mark 4 is not changed here. For context (computed here, suggested): under no change, the absolute rule (loops:0 at most 5 on every seed) passes about 6 percent of the time over six seeds, and a six-seed mean at most 5 passes about 85 percent (resampling the eight stored B2 values, which came from different training runs, so this is rough). Mark 4 therefore mostly fails by seed noise. That is a reason for Ben to decide on a separate amendment, not a reason to restate it here. plan.autonomy: Test-side only. This probe is not a method of the deployed model and changes nothing the model does at run time. The zero-round path is a lesion used only in tests. The probe sets no runtime value, gate or threshold, and its floors come from train rows only, so no dev answer picks a floor. It is researcher scoring, which rule 1 allows for tests. If a later change makes the model choose its own route or stop its own thinking, that change is a new method and needs its own rule-10 check: the model must choose from its own tries with no researcher step at deploy time.

Shown (I read ledger.py run/talk and the RESULT.json files): at zero rounds the controller state comes only from parameters, so the mode head gives one route per checkpoint. The real fix to mark 4 (88-94% rejection of an identical design) is a wording and mark-form choice that only Ben can make, sealed before any confirm. That choice does not wait on this probe. If the data are being copied to a machine for another job anyway, add loops:0 to the planned eval-only --save-preds re-run of the saved checkpoints. Better, use route identity plus per-family counts as the gate. Measure CPU fp32 against the stored CUDA bf16 count on one checkpoint first (untested). Add s202, s204 and s205 to the gate set; their stored counts (0, 48, 0) reproduce from RESULT.json (shown).

The untrained-init floor is the wrong chance floor. An untrained B2 picks an arbitrary route and will almost surely score near 0 to 2%, so the rule 'either init above 5% means mark 4 sits at or below chance' will almost never fire. That makes the stage near-null, not a test. The rule 'a trained checkpoint that does not exceed the untrained floor is at chance' is also vacuous for the seeds that store 0. Restore the floor the earlier plan had: the best constant or majority answer per family, chosen on train rows only and scored on dev, plus the candidate-count chance (prompt numbers plus constants for a number route, prompt words for a word route). Report an untrained init at most as a wiring check.

Do not state the one-route prediction as 'identical output'. Only the mode head is row-independent (shown). The NUM and WORD picks use row-dependent keys, and the write-out route reads the reader output through the copy keys, so its string can vary by row. Report the route histogram, the argmax slot and word-index histogram and the distinct write-out strings, and judge only 'more than 1% of rows on a different mode'. Count every fallback to write-out: a word index past the row's word list, a row with no words, and an invalid number pointer.

Class C (computed) is route-conditional and cannot be hit on a number or word route except by coincidence with a prompt number, constant or word. Report it only for write-out checkpoints and never read a low value as support for the thinker and executor account on other seeds. The 0.24-0.82 noexec floor comes from the 6,800-row big build with the intact controller, so use it as a reference only.

idea.title: Twin-run noise floor and a three-tier equivalence gate
idea.summary: Every speed rewrite needs a way to show it did not change the math, and nobody knows how much a plain GPU rerun differs from itself. Run same-seed twins on one machine, log software versions and code hashes into RESULT.json, and adopt a three-tier gate: bitwise for host-side edits, a 1e-5 fp32 CPU check for rounding-level edits, a loss-curve-inside-the-floor check on GPU. Only batch-composition or schedule changes then need 6 paired seeds.
idea.change: No model change. (a) CPU: rerun the existing 60-step determinism check (test_harness.py:113) for the B2 config (copy=True, scatter_add_ path) with one thread. (b) PC: B2 seed 200 twice and plain_tf seed 200 twice, --steps 1000 --log-every 50 --final-eval off; compare all 20 logged losses and a state_dict hash; log torch, CUDA, cuDNN, GPU name, ledger.py hash and data manifest hash. problems: [shown] The gate floor comes from one same-config pair per arm, so it has one degree of freedom. The idea's own cross-box pair (+0.48 and +0.12 pooled-5) gives a sample SD of 0.26 with a 95% range of roughly 0.12 to 8 (recomputed), which the idea admits bounds nothing. A floor from one same-config pair has the same weakness.

[suggested, arithmetic] With one twin pair the floor is a single draw. If a rewrite adds only noise of the twin's size, P(|new diff| <= |twin diff|) is 1/2 at each logged point. The rule requires every point to pass, so equivalent rewrites would fail often. A multiplier or a floor from several pairs must be fixed before the runs.

[shown in the idea] Pass rules cover only bit-equal twins or all points within relative 1e-3. The proved-wrong line covers only differences above 1% by update 200. Twins that differ by between 1e-3 and 1% get no verdict, and no basis is given for the 1e-3 band. The orchestrator note says the band must not be picked after seeing the twins.

[shown in the idea; suggested for the mechanism] The Tier 1 threshold (1e-5 relative on loss and parameters after 5 CPU fp32 steps) and the Tier 2 threshold (0.5 points on 1,000 dev rows) are not derived from any measured floor. D7 measures only identical-config reruns, but speed edits change arithmetic order (padding width, kernels), and that perturbation floor is never measured. AdamW with default eps 1e-8 (train.py:150) can turn tiny rounding differences in near-zero-gradient coordinates into steps of about the learning rate, so a parameter-level 1e-5 check may fail an equivalent edit. Untested here (torch is not installed).

[shown] The 1e-5 fp32 equivalence test already exists in the plan as 8A-SPEC section 12, G2 (whole-model-roadmap/8A-SPEC-2026-10-07.md lines 369-375): loss and gradients within 1e-5 plus the same predictions on 1,000 dev rows. D7 says it 'generalises' G2 but does not reuse it or add its padding-width test, which is the test that matters for speed edits.

[shown] Wrong shape. The twins are q33 B2 (8 loops, 9 registers, 27 slots). The rewrite the gate is meant to certify is G2 on the 8a shape (12 rounds, 36 registers, 106 slots; 8A-SPEC lines 361 and 374-377). A floor measured on one shape does not transfer to the other.

[shown in the idea] Tier 0 says 'hash of the first 500 batches'. A hash of row ids or prompt tensors does not catch a changed target. Host-side rewrites (collate in data.py:119-143, gold() in ledger.py:433-454) change exactly the target tensors and weights that the loss consumes, so the hash must cover those tensors.

[shown] The closest prior is incomplete, and step (a) is not a rerun. tests/test_ledger_copy.py (test_copy_false_is_B) and tests/test_ledger_span.py (test_span_false_is_b2) already check the current B2 code against recorded fingerprints on a 48-row batch (loss within 1e-4, weight sums within 1e-8 relative). test_harness.py trains --model plain_tf at d_model 64 with 2 layers, not the B2 copy=True path, so the B2 check is a new test.

[shown] '--final-eval off' is an invalid command: train.py:121 defines --final-eval as store_true, so 'off' is an argparse error. Without final eval the twins have no dev-check floor for the Tier 2 0.5-point check.

[shown] Timing mismatch. Twins log every 50 steps over 1,000 steps (20 points, from train.py:176). Tier 2 checks 200 steps every 20 steps, which has no floor point at that spacing. A floor from 1,000-step divergence also does not describe 200-step divergence.

[shown] Stage (d) touches a sealed rung that is already running. Addendum H (8A-SPEC lines 385-402) runs seeds 400-405 on one 5090 per seed, and whole-model-roadmap/8a-results/ already holds per-seed folders for at least 401, 402 and 405 (created 21:21-21:27 UTC on 10-07). Nothing in custom_io sets cudnn.benchmark, TF32 or deterministic flags (grep finds only the scatter_add_ at ledger.py:248), so co-tenancy should change speed, not values. Keep reference copies for the deployed path, or confine rewrites to a build-only entry point.

DEV GATE MUST NOT MOVE INTO THE MODEL [shown for the pattern; runtime use untested]: Tier 2's 1,000-row dev check is allowed at build time, but rule 10 bars dev-tuned gates at run time. fastsleep/creative/fastsleep.py lines 45-51 already build dev floors from dev rows in setup. Whether the nightly loop reads them was not checked here. The twin gate must stay out of that path.

COMMAND ERROR [shown]: '--final-eval off' is invalid. train.py line 121 defines --final-eval with action='store_true', so argparse rejects the extra token 'off'; the flag must be omitted. The twin command also omits --bf16 (train.py line 118). The confirm RESULT.json configs record bf16 True and device auto (results/33-pc-confirm-b2/B2_s200/RESULT.json), so the twins must match that config, not only the seed.

THREE PASS MARKS, NO DECISION BETWEEN THEM [shown in the idea text]: pass_mark is bit-equal, or all points within relative 1e-3; Tier 2 says 'inside the twin floor' (the spread of the twins themselves); proved_wrong is any pair over 1% by update 200. Nothing says what happens between 1e-3 and 1%. Rule 4 needs one number fixed in writing before the twins run, with the outcome for every case.

FLOOR NOT MEASURED AT THE GATE'S RESOLUTION [shown]: the twins log every 50 steps over 1,000 steps (train.py line 176 logs when step % log_every == 0, giving 20 points). Tier 2 checks a 200-step curve every 20 steps, which the twin logs never produce. The logged loss is a mean over each log window (train.py lines 175-180), so a 20-step gate needs --log-every 20 in the twins.

ONE PAIR CANNOT SET A FLOOR [shown + computed]: the 1-df SD of 0.26 comes from two cross-machine differences (+0.48 and +0.12, results/RESULTS-EG2.md line 125). Its 95% range is about 0.12 to 8.3 (computed from the chi-square with 1 df). The idea's own 'why' says this bounds nothing, yet Tier 2 uses it as the gate. Rule 4 needs 6 paired seeds for any claim, and a noise floor is one. Use 6 B2 twin pairs (seeds 200-205) or drop the band and keep only bitwise and CPU fp32 checks.

TIER 0 MISSES THE TARGETS [shown]: a hash of the first 500 batches covers the data batch only. The teacher-forcing targets are built on the host in ledger.gold() (ledger.py lines 433-455, called from loss() at line 499): op, a, b, mode, ans, word, gen and has, plus the loss weight w_row (line 501). A host-side rewrite of gold() could change the targets and still pass Tier 0. The gate must hash the gold() dict and weights at each step.

TIER 1 IS NOT THE G2 STANDARD [shown]: the idea cites 'G2 standard', but 8A-SPEC section 12 (whole-model-roadmap/8A-SPEC-2026-10-07.md lines 369-375) asks for loss and gradients at relative 1e-5 in fp32, plus identical predictions on 1,000 dev rows. The idea tests loss and parameters after 5 steps and drops gradients.

THE EXISTING DETERMINISM CHECK COVERS plain_tf ONLY [shown]: test_harness.py lines 97-113 run plain_tf (d_model 64, CPU, 60 steps) and compare final_train_loss from a second in-process run. They do not touch copy=True or ledger.py, and one process says little about cross-process repeatability. The B2 check has to be written new; it is not an existing check.

NO PROVENANCE FIELDS EXIST [shown]: RESULT.json keys (checked on results/33-pc-confirm-b2/B2_s200 and results/40-egw-s200/B2V_s200) hold no torch, CUDA, cuDNN, GPU name or code hash. train.py lines 195-198 record a data hash only when a MANIFEST.json sits in --data. DETERMINISTIC-MODE BRANCH IS UNDEFINED [suggested; torch is not installed here, so untested]: ledger.py line 248 is the only scatter_add_ in custom_io (grep, shown). plain_tf.py lines 116 and 125 use non-add scatter_ calls, which the idea cites but does not discuss. It should state the fallback: CPU fp32 for equivalence, and 6 paired seeds for any non-bitwise change.

SAME CARD STATE IS NOT ENFORCEABLE [shown, from the brief and the local_runner docstring]: the 5070 Ti is shared with another thread and gated only by free memory. Record nvidia-smi and co-tenant state in each twin log rather than assuming 'same card state per pair'.

UNNAMED INPUTS AND CONSTANTS [shown]: the '1,000-row dev check' names no split or row list. Name a dev split, never GOLD-PRIVATE or blind (rule 5). STAGE (d) NEEDS BEN'S OK [shown in rules]: rented replicates (the idea estimates about $2.9) are allowed only when the PC and Mac are both full (rule 6). Keep stage (d) optional and do not start it on the model's behalf.

problems: Tier 2 band is either zero or a single sample, so the gate is bitwise or close to a coin flip. If the twins are bit-equal (the pass_mark's first branch), the floor is 0 and every GPU float-order edit fails Tier 2. If they are not bit-equal, the floor is the deviation of one twin pair. Under exchangeability a fresh equivalent edit passes with probability k/(k+1) for k pairs: 0.50 at k=1, 0.75 at k=3, 0.90 at k=9 (suggested arithmetic). The second branch uses a fixed relative 1e-3 band that no measurement supports, and it conflicts with Tier 2's 'twin floor' wording.

Tier 1 misquotes the standard it cites. 8A-SPEC-2026-10-07.md section 12 (G2, around lines 369-375) asks for loss and gradients at relative 1e-5 in fp32, plus the same predictions on 1,000 dev rows. D7 compares loss and parameters after 5 AdamW steps. Adam's update is lr*g/(|g|+1e-8), so a parameter whose gradient sits near eps can move by roughly lr times reorder-noise divided by eps, far above 1e-5 relative (suggested from the update rule; untested). Tier 1 is also CPU fp32, while training uses bf16 autocast only on CUDA (train.py:118). It does not exercise the kernels whose reorder noise matters for GPU speed edits.

Shown: the claim 'no same-seed replicate of any B2 run exists' misses two same-config rented pairs. first-look-10m-results/B2_s200 vs results/40-egw-s200/B2V_s200 gives pooled-5 73.39 vs 73.48 and final 500-step train loss 0.01285 vs 0.01682 (31% apart). B2_s201 vs B2V_s201 gives pooled-5 74.93 vs 74.39 (diff 0.54) and loss 0.01202 vs 0.02377 (98% apart). Configs match except save_preds and the out path. These are the closest replicate data available and should be the first floor samples. Their one-df SDs are 0.06 and 0.38 (pooled 0.27 on 2 df), so they are rough.

Shown: the cross-box comparison is confounded by OS, data path and code revision, not just the box. The PC RESULT.json configs have no max_ans or english_eval keys, which the rented configs have. The PC data path is C:\Users\benja\custom-io\work\data and its stdout shows Windows torch paths, while the rented runs use /job/data on Linux. The idea lists box, data path and max_ans but not OS or code revision, so the 20% and 71% final-loss gaps cannot be attributed to GPU nondeterminism.

Shown: the loss signal is far noisier than the score. Identical-config rented runs differ by 31% and 98% in final train loss but by only 0.09 and 0.54 in pooled-5. A loss-curve band and a relative 1e-3 band are therefore more likely to reject equivalent runs than to certify them. Whether the 200-step loss behaves the same way is untested.

Shown: the existing determinism check is weaker than cited. test_harness.py:97 and :113 train plain_tf (d_model 64, 60 steps, CPU) and compare one final_train_loss. They do not run the B2 config (copy=True), compare parameters, or check the logged points. The B2-specific equivalence mechanism already in the repo is tests/test_ledger_copy.py and tests/test_ledger_span.py: fingerprints of init and seed-0 loss with a 1e-4 absolute loss tolerance and 1e-8 relative weight sums. The loss check there is skipped when train.jsonl's size differs. D7 should reuse these and not cite test_harness as its closest prior.
Shown: step (b)'s command is invalid. train.py:121 defines --final-eval with action='store_true', so '--final-eval off' is an argparse error. The flag should be omitted.

Shown: step (d)'s cost is understated about 3 to 4 times. D7 says six replicate boxes cost about $2.90. 8A-SPEC-2026-10-07.md line 94 sets the 3M cap at $2.50 per box after addendum B3, section 18 (lines 396-401) gives $3.30 per box, and it expects 3-4 hours a box and about $11 in all. At $0.49/h, six boxes come to about $9-12. Also, the 8a 3M shape is not today's q33 B2: G3 (8A lines ~378-380) gives 12 rounds, 44 controller tokens and up to 280 letters. Replicates of the 8a shape do not measure the B2 that the speed work would edit (suggested).

Suggested: 1,000-step twins and 200-step curves cannot show whether a float-order edit changes the 24k dev score that the marks read. The proposed 'dev check within 0.5' has no measured floor, because the twin protocol runs with final eval off. The gate would certify only early trajectories unless one edit is also checked against its reference at 12k or 24k on dev.

Suggested: the proved-wrong condition (any twin pair differs by more than 1% by update 200) measures GPU noise, not whether the gate works. The idea has no positive or negative controls. A known-equivalent edit, such as widening the padding (ConvBlock masks padding at reader.py:49-51), should pass. A known-different edit, such as a one-slot result remap error or a 1e-3 perturbation, should fail. False-reject and false-pass rates should be measured from those.

Suggested: the 'same card state' control does not protect numerics. Co-tenant processes change timing, not per-kernel results, although memory pressure could change cuDNN or cuBLAS algorithm choice (untested) and risks OOM. The real controls are the same software, the same frozen code copy and the same data manifest, run back to back.

Shown: the nondeterminism candidates are incomplete and one citation is off. ledger.py:248 scatter_add_ (in gen_copy, with repeated character indices) is a real atomic-add candidate. But plain_tf.py:116 and :125 use scatter_ with unique indices, so they are not evidence that plain_tf has no scatter_add. The reader's two Conv1d blocks (reader.py:43-51) are a second candidate for cuDNN backward, and grep finds no cudnn.deterministic or benchmark setting anywhere in custom_io (shown absence). The step (c) deterministic run should record every op that raises, not only ledger.py:248.

Shown, and the claim is too broad: on the ledger side padding changes are not only float order. The reader and pools are masked, so reader padding is invariant in math (reader.py:49-51; ledger.py:291 pool uses spans). But 8A G2 says a slot-count change moves result-slot indices and needs a remap, so Tier 0 and Tier 1 must catch remap errors, not only rounding.

Shown (minor): the 95% range for the one-df SD from +0.48 and +0.12 is about 0.11 to 8.1, not 0.12 to 8.2. The per-split offsets (in_dist -0.51/-1.03, vocab +1.63/+1.87) reproduce. The '4 of 4 rented-above-PC on pooled-5' count reproduces only when the first-look runs are included, and per-split direction is mixed (6 of 10 positive).

Scheduling: the 0.6 h is compute only. The brief says the PC queue is full (queue 39 ETA about 9 PM ET, queues 40-44 after it), so the twins would wait behind them. This is from the brief and was not re-checked in the queue files.
critiques.rescue: Keep the measurement stage and hold the gate until its tiers are rewritten. (1) Run 4 to 5 B2 twin pairs at 1,000 steps on the PC back to back, with the same frozen code copy and data manifest, --log-every 50 and no --final-eval flag. Log the 20 points, a parameter hash, and torch, CUDA, cuDNN, GPU, OS and code hash. (2) If the twins are bit-equal, use bitwise checks for host-side edits only, and treat GPU float-order edits as needing a 6-seed run. If they are not, set the band before any speed edit as the max over the pairs times a fixed factor, and report the false-reject rate using extra twin pairs as known-equivalent controls. (3) Add planted controls: padding widening must pass, and a one-slot remap error must fail. (4) Make Tier 1 match G2: compare loss and pre-optimizer gradients in fp64 on CPU, plus predictions on 1,000 dev rows, and compare parameters only after normalizing by update size. (5) Require one 12k dev twin check of any accepted GPU edit against its reference. (6) Add the two rented same-config pairs (first-look vs B2V, seeds 200 and 201) as extra floor samples and report their loss spread. (7) Fix the --final-eval flag, correct the cost to about $9-12, and cite tests/test_ledger_copy.py and tests/test_ledger_span.py as the closest prior.
critiques.already_tried: Closest prior, all checked in files: test_harness.py:97-113 (plain_tf, CPU, 60 steps, final_train_loss equality only); tests/test_ledger_copy.py and tests/test_ledger_span.py (B2-code fingerprints at seed 0, loss within 1e-4 absolute, weight sums within 1e-8 relative, loss check skipped when train.jsonl size differs); whole-model-roadmap/first-look-10m-results/B2_s200 and B2_s201 against results/40-egw-s200/B2V_s200 and results/41-egw-s201/B2V_s201 (same config, both rented, not cited by the idea); results/RESULTS-EG2.md device check (cross-box, confounded by OS, data path and code revision); no-hardcoding/D0b-RESULT-2026-10-07.md (CPU fp32 eval reproduces plain_tf_steps scores exactly, eval only, no training); 8A-SPEC G2 (fp32 1e-5 test on loss and gradients, a standard the idea says it generalises but does not match).
critiques.expected_effect: Verification infrastructure only: no change to any score, speed or mark. If the gate works, each equivalent speed edit that would otherwise need a 6-seed B2 check is avoided. That check is about 9 run-hours, or about 3 wall-hours at par 3 on the brief's packing estimate. With a one-pair floor the gate passes about half of equivalent edits (suggested), so the saving is roughly halved. The twin stage costs about 1 to 2 PC-hours for 4 to 5 pairs, plus queue wait, so it is worth running only after the floor has that many pairs and the controls are in place. It does not make B2 train faster by itself.

problems: Test order does not match the cheapest decisive question. Design step (b) is two 1000-step B2 runs (about 0.5 h, behind the PC queue). A 20-step GPU twin with a per-step loss and a parameter hash costs minutes (suggested, from the shown 1.6 to 6.7 updates/s) and answers the first question: is bit-exact GPU equality reachable at all. The 1000-step pairs are needed only if it is not.

The pass and fail rules leave a gap. Pass is bit-equal or all points within relative 1e-3. Proved-wrong is any pair above 1%. Nothing is assigned between 1e-3 and 1%. bf16 autocast (shown: train.py line 132, CUDA only) has unit roundoff about 0.4% (arithmetic), so same-code GPU twins are plausibly in that gap. The proved-wrong clause also does not test the idea: a wide gate is a result, not a refutation.

One twin pair is a one-degree-of-freedom floor, and the design's own arithmetic shows it bounds little (its SD 0.26 has a 95% range of about 0.1 to 8; recomputed shown: 0.11 to 8.1). Under exchangeability, a rewrite with no math change lands inside a one-pair floor about half the time at a given point (suggested). The project has already seen no-change null checks fail (PASS-MARKS addenda 19; analyze_gain null_check). The design has no null check and no known-equal or known-different control for its gate.

Wrong length for the floor. --steps 1000 changes the lr curve (lr_at takes args.steps), so the floor comes from a compressed 1000-step cosine, not the 24k recipe used by the B2 confirm and the 8a 3M rung (shown: 8a-results B2 runs are 24,000 steps). Twin divergence usually grows with training (suggested), so a 200 to 1000 step floor may understate the 24k deviation. Nothing in the design covers 24k.

Tier 1 cannot see the bf16 path. Tier 1 is CPU fp32, and autocast is CUDA-only (shown). The speed edits most likely to change rounding (batch shapes, fused kernels) are therefore judged only at Tier 2, which has the one-pair floor. The 'G2 standard' is also misdescribed: 8A-SPEC G2 is in Addendum G (section 17, not section 12 as the brief says) and asks for loss and gradients plus predictions on 1,000 dev rows, not parameters after 5 steps.

Rule 4 is brushed past. Tier 2 gates on a 1,000-row dev score within 0.5 from one pair. That is a score-equivalence claim, which rule 4 puts at six seeds; otherwise it should be labelled a math check with the dev number reported only. The 0.5 band is also smaller than the shown rented-minus-PC pooled-5 offsets (+0.12, +0.39, +0.48, +0.66), so identical math run on a rented box would fail the gate. Ben should rule on whether equivalence checks count under rule 4.

Step (d) is mis-specified. Seeds 400-405 are the sealed 8a 3M rung (8A-SPEC section 5 and section 18). B2 8a results already exist for 401, 402 and 405 (shown: 8a-results/*-B2/RESULT.json). The 8a B2 shape (12 loops, 36 registers, 106 slots; shown in box.json) differs from q33's. No PC run exists for those seeds, so 'paired by seed with the original boxes' compares rented with rented and cannot measure PC-versus-rented drift. The useful pairing is seeds 200-205 with the q33 config on 5090s (shown $0.48/h in box.json; about $3 for six B2-only boxes, arithmetic), matched to the six PC confirm runs. The four rented-minus-PC pooled-5 differences are all positive, which suggests a systematic offset (suggested; only two PC reference runs, so weak).

The B2 shape is unstated. The design says 'B2 seed 200', but the speed work targets whichever B2 runs. q33 is 8 loops, 9 registers, 27 slots; the 8a B2 is 12 loops, 36 registers, 106 slots, and G3 says the bigger shape is slower per update. A floor measured on one shape does not transfer to the other. Each floor should name the config it covers.

The existing check is weaker than described. test_harness.py line 112 runs plain_tf, not B2, on CPU only, and asserts equality of one scalar (final_train_loss). The design presents it as the B2 config check. It must be extended and reported as a new check. It says nothing about GPU behaviour.

The nondeterminism source is only partly identified. ledger.py:248 (scatter_add_) is the only scatter_add in the models (shown; plain_tf uses scatter_ at lines 116 and 125, which is consistent with the design). Other CUDA ops on the B2 path are candidates (suggested, untested): cuDNN Conv1d backward in reader.py ConvBlock, nn.Embedding backward, and attention backward. Testing scatter_add_ alone will not settle bitwise equality. The 'same card state' requirement has no stated mechanism; if it matters, say why (suggested: cuDNN algorithm choice can depend on free workspace).

The hours ignore the queue. The '0.6 h' is run time only. Queues 39 to 44 hold about 18 runs at 24k steps (shown in the queue_local headers), and at the shown speeds that is more than 10 hours of PC time (estimate). Only the CPU stage and a short GPU stage fit before tomorrow unless the test is inserted ahead of the queue or run on a rented box.

Tier 0 is underspecified. A hash of the first 500 batches covers only the data rows. Host-side edits can change gold() targets and token caches (ledger.py gold(); spans cache cleared at 20,000 entries), so the hash must cover the full model.loss inputs, including targets.
critiques.rescue: Staged, cheapest first, with the decision rule written before any run. Stage 0 (CPU, minutes): Tier 0 hash over the full loss inputs (rows and gold targets) for the first 500 batches; extend the determinism check to B2 (copy=True) for 20 steps, comparing per-step losses and a state_dict hash on one thread. Stage 1 (PC, minutes, two short B2 jobs at about 5 GB): GPU twins, seed 200, q33 config, 20 steps, per-step loss and parameter hash, once with defaults and once with use_deterministic_algorithms(True), cudnn.deterministic and CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG; record any raise. If bitwise equal, GPU speed edits are gated by bit equality and need no floor. If not, record the per-step divergence curve. Stage 2 (PC, only if Stage 1 diverges): at least three twin pairs with the real 24k schedule, stopped at 1000 steps by a new stop flag in train.py (outside the model), plus one full 24k twin pair to calibrate the 24k floor. Gate: a rewrite passes if its deviation at every logged point is no larger than the largest twin-pair deviation at that point; no intermediate band. Before any speed edit is judged, a known-equal control (for example fixed-width padding against batch-max padding) must pass and a known-different control (shuffled batch order) must fail. Stage 3 (rented, optional, needs Ben's OK): six B2 runs on seeds 200-205 with the q33 config on 5090s, paired with the six PC confirm runs, to measure box offset; not seeds 400-405. Logging: add torch, CUDA, cuDNN, GPU name, git commit, ledger.py hash and manifest hash to RESULT.json and box.json, and name the B2 shape each floor covers. Drop the dev-score band from Tier 2 or report it only.
critiques.already_tried: Existing: test_harness.py line 112, a CPU plain_tf 60-step same-seed scalar check (not GPU, not B2). No same-seed GPU replicate exists for B2 or plain_tf in results/ (shown). Cross-box same-seed pairs exist: pooled-5 +0.48 and +0.12 (results 40 and 41 against 33) and +0.39 and +0.66 (first-look-10m-results/readout.json machine offsets); all four favour the rented box, from two PC reference runs. 8A-SPEC Addendum G item G2 is a 1e-5 fp32 check for per-batch slot sizing, the same idea for one edit, not a noise floor. No determinism flags anywhere in custom_io (grep: none). Verified as stated: ledger.py:248 is the only scatter_add in models; ConvBlock masks padding (reader.py lines 49-51); B2_s200 RESULT.json has no torch, GPU or code hash; 8a box dph 0.48; the one-degree-of-freedom SD reproduces within rounding (about 0.25; 95% range about 0.11 to 8.1). Closest prior: none found for a GPU twin floor.
critiques.expected_effect: Stages 0 and 1 cost under 0.2 h of PC time (minutes if a gap opens) and say whether bit-exact GPU equality holds, which decides whether most speed edits need any floor. If equality fails, Stage 2 costs roughly 1 to 5 h of PC time depending on whether 24k pairs are needed, and the rented offset check costs about $3. The idea adds no speed or score by itself; its value is letting speed edits be certified without a six-seed run, which holds only if Ben rules that math-equivalence checks are not score claims under rule 4. Nothing in the design makes a score claim, and as written the gate would likely reject identical math about half the time per point, so it should not be used until the controls pass.

chair.reasons:
Worth a small sealed test, but not as written. No rule is broken: it is a build-time check with no model change, no new data, no protected panels and no deploy-time step (rule 10 clean, apart from one shared-code caveat below). The question is real and unmeasured: how far apart are two same-seed, same-code runs on one GPU? Every speed edit (host-side rewrite, per-batch slot sizing, CUDA graphs, torch.compile) needs a way to show it did not change the math without a 6-seed rerun (about 9 run-hours). Cost is minutes of PC time if the first stage is cut down.

I checked these against the files. SHOWN: train.py:121 defines --final-eval as store_true, so the proposed '--final-eval off' is an argparse error, and the twins must also pass --bf16 and --max-ans 8 to match the confirm config (results/33-pc-confirm-b2/B2_s200/RESULT.json config: bf16 True, max_ans None on the PC, 8 on the rented runs). SHOWN: test_harness.py:97-113 trains plain_tf (d_model 64, 60 steps, CPU) and compares one scalar, final_train_loss, so it is not the B2 copy=True path and is not a GPU check. SHOWN: tests/test_ledger_copy.py and tests/test_ledger_span.py already pin the current B2 code to fingerprints on a 48-row batch (per the critics; the files exist in custom_io/tests). SHOWN: 8A-SPEC G2 is in Addendum G (section 17, not section 12) and asks for loss and gradients within 1e-5 relative in fp32 plus identical predictions on 1,000 dev rows. It does not ask for parameters after 5 AdamW steps, so Tier 1 as written misquotes it. SHOWN: Addendum H (section 18) puts 8a seeds 400-405 on one rented 5090 per seed, at about $3.30 a box and about $11 total, so stage (d) touches a sealed rung and its $2.9 cost is understated. Drop stage (d).

CORRECTION to the idea's premise (SHOWN, recomputed from RESULT.json): same-seed, same-config B2 reruns DO exist. Seed 200 on three runs: PC q33 73.00 (final train loss 0.02098), rented B2V 73.48 (0.01682), first-look B2 73.39 (0.01285). Seed 201: 74.27 (0.0139), 74.39 (0.02377), 74.93 (0.01202). The two rented runs per seed share bf16, max_ans 8, device auto, batch 256, order shuffled and data path /job/data. Their pooled-5 differs by only 0.09 and 0.54, while the 500-step-mean final train loss is 31% and 98% apart. Whether the two rented runs used the same code revision, the same torch version, or the same co-tenant load is not recorded (no version or hash in any RESULT.json), so GPU nondeterminism is suggested, not isolated. Two consequences. (1) A relative 1e-3 loss band cannot hold at 24k steps; at that length same-config runs are already far outside it. If a loss band exists it can only apply to early steps. (2) The score is much less noisy than the loss, so a loss-curve gate would reject equivalent edits while pooled-5 would hardly move. The gate should therefore be graded by tier, and only the early-step bitwise and CPU tiers should be exact.

DEFECTS TO FIX BEFORE ANY RUN (all SHOWN by the critics' file checks, which agree): (a) one twin pair is a one-degree-of-freedom floor. The cross-box SD of 0.26 from two differences has a 95% range of about 0.11 to 8.1, and under exchangeability a fresh equivalent edit lands inside a k-pair floor with probability k/(k+1) (0.50 at k=1), so equivalent edits would fail about half the time. (b) The pass mark (bit-equal or within 1e-3), the proved-wrong line (above 1% by update 200) and Tier 2 ('inside the twin floor') leave no verdict between 1e-3 and 1%, and bf16 rounding of about 0.4% sits in that gap. (c) The 1e-3 and 0.5-point numbers have no derivation and may have been picked to fit; they must be fixed now or derived from measured pairs by a rule fixed now. (d) Twins log every 50 steps but Tier 2 checks every 20, so the floor is not measured at the gate's resolution. (e) Tier 0 hashes only the batch, but host-side rewrites (collate, ledger.gold(), ledger.py:433-454 and the weights at 501) change the targets, so the hash must cover ids, masks, gold targets and the row weights. (f) The shape is q33 (8 rounds, 9 registers, 27 slots) but G2 will be applied to the 8a shape (12 rounds, 36 registers, 106 slots), so each floor must name the shape it covers. (g) The idea has no positive or negative control; a gate that never failed a known-different edit has not been shown to work. (h) 'Same card state' is not enforceable on the shared card (coordination is free memory and GPU-BUSY.txt only); log nvidia-smi and co-tenant state and test directly with one twin alone and one under a co-tenant instead of assuming. (i) The name 'twin' already means the plain baseline in this repo (design/design-workspace-typed.md, design/JUDGES.md); call them 'same-config reruns'. (j) AdamW at eps 1e-8 can turn rounding-size gradient differences in near-zero-gradient coordinates into steps of about lr, so comparing parameters after Adam steps is the wrong CPU check; compare loss and pre-optimizer gradients (suggested, untested).

AUTONOMY CAVEAT (SHOWN by the autonomy critic): the fast-sleep nightly loop imports collate, to_device and lr_at from custom_io and ledger.execute and value_code in its sampler and legal modules. A rewrite of those functions for training speed would reach the deployed sleep path without being checked by D7. Fix: speed edits go in a build-only entry point or the gate also covers the sleep imports; the sleep path keeps reference copies. The 1,000-row dev check is a build-time check and must never become a runtime gate.

SEQUENCING: this is infrastructure; it speeds nothing by itself and pays only when a speed edit exists. It should run after, or alongside, the one-step profile and the par-1/2/3 throughput measurement (the Director's ideas 1 and 3), since those decide which edits are worth building. The GPU part must be short enough to slot ahead of queue 39 or into a gap: the 0.6 h in the idea is run time only and the PC queue is full.
chair.revised_idea:
Method-D7 revised: a same-config rerun floor and a tiered equivalence gate, measured in stages that stop as soon as the answer is known. No model change, params cost 0, no deploy-time step. Name 'same-config rerun' (not 'twin').

STAGE 0, CPU, free, minutes (torch is not installed here, so this is a plan for Ben's machines). New B2 test (copy=True, scatter_add_ path, 8 rounds, q33 shape): one thread, fp32, 20 steps, same seed. Run twice in one process and twice in separate processes. Log per-step loss and a sha256 of the state_dict. Reuse the fingerprints in tests/test_ledger_copy.py and tests/test_ledger_span.py. Keep the test_harness.py step as plain_tf only. Pass (fixed now): per-step losses and the hash are bit-equal. If not equal, stop: the test itself or a hidden CPU nondeterminism needs fixing first.

STAGE 1, PC, minutes. Frozen code copy and data manifest, the q33 B2 confirm command: --bf16 --device auto --max-ans 8, same --data and --vocab, seed 200, --steps 200 --warmup 20 --log-every 1, no --final-eval flag. Run A, then B, back to back. Log per-step loss, sha256 of checkpoint.pt weights at the end, torch/CUDA/cuDNN/GPU/OS, hashes of ledger.py, train.py, data.py and the manifest, and an nvidia-smi sample every 5 s. Add one rerun C under a co-tenant. Then repeat A,B with torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True) (warn_only off), CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG=:4096:8 and cudnn.deterministic; record every op that raises (ledger.py:248 scatter_add_ and the Conv1d and Embedding backward are candidates) and patch nothing. Outcomes fixed in advance: (i) A and B bit-equal at all 200 steps and equal weight hash, C also equal: GPU bitwise gate exists; host-side edits must be bit-equal. Float-order GPU edits then need the Stage 2 floor. (ii) A and B differ: record the per-step divergence curve and go to Stage 2. (iii) A and C differ while A and B do not: card state matters; log it for every later comparison.

STAGE 2, only if (ii) or float-order edits are to be gated. At least 5 same-config rerun pairs (seeds 200-204), 1,000 steps, --log-every 20, with a new --stop-at flag so the lr follows the real 24k schedule (a --steps 1000 run compresses the cosine and gives a different floor; add the flag outside the model). Hold 2 extra pairs (seed 205 and one more) as held-out controls. Gate rule fixed now: an edit passes if its deviation from its same-seed reference at every logged step is at most 2 times the largest deviation seen across the 5 pairs at that step; no band is left without a verdict. Report the false-reject rate on the held-out pairs. Add one 24k same-config pair per shape in use (q33 and 8a shape) to calibrate the full-length floor, since same-config pooled-5 is known to differ by 0.09 and 0.54 and the final loss by 31% and 98% (rented, seeds 200 and 201). Free extra floor samples already on disk: the PC / B2V / first-look triples for seeds 200 and 201.

PLANTED CONTROLS before any edit is judged: known-equal (batch padded to 161 instead of 81 characters; fixed-width padding vs batch-max padding) must pass; known-different (shuffled batch order, or a one-slot result remap error, or a 1e-3 weight perturbation) must fail. A gate that fails either control is not used.

THE GATE TIERS: Tier 0 (host-side edits to data.py collate/to_device, ledger.gold, tokenize/spans caches): sha256 over the full loss inputs (ids, masks, place codes, gold dict, w_row, lr) for the first 500 batches, bitwise. Tier 1 (math-level edits such as per-batch slot sizing, padding width): the G2 test exactly as 8A-SPEC section 17 words it: CPU fp32 (fp64 preferred), loss and pre-optimizer gradients within 1e-5 relative on real pool batches, plus identical predictions on 1,000 rows of a NAMED dev split (in_dist dev; never GOLD-PRIVATE or blind); report, do not claim, scores. Tier 2 (GPU numerics edits: torch.compile, fused kernels, bf16 changes): the Stage 2 rule above, plus a 200-step curve check at the measured resolution. Tier 3 (needs 6 paired seeds under rule 4): length-bucketed or packed batches, any schedule or --minutes change, any change in data order.

LOGGING (do first, because the hashes must name the code actually tested): write torch, CUDA, cuDNN, GPU name, OS, ledger.py/train.py/data.py hashes, data manifest hash, nvidia-smi sample and --max-ans into RESULT.json. local_runner.py already names each frozen code copy by a hash, so reuse that value.

DROPPED: stage (d), the six rented replicates on seeds 400-405 (a sealed rung; ask separately, and if wanted use seeds 200-205 on the q33 config, about $3 for B2 only, to measure box offset, with Ben's OK). Dropped: the 0.5-point dev band as a gate (report only). Dropped: '--final-eval off'. Added to sequencing: run after the one-step profile and the par-1/2/3 throughput test; keep speed rewrites of collate/to_device/lr_at/execute out of the fast-sleep import path.
chair.plan_guidance: The test plan must get these right. (1) Pre-register in one place, before any run, a single outcome table with no gap: Stage 1 outcomes (bit-equal / differ / differ only under co-tenant), the Stage 2 gate rule (deviation at every logged step at most 2x the largest of at least 5 same-config pair deviations at that step), and what each outcome means for which edits need which tier. The old text's 1e-3 pass band, >1% proved-wrong line and 'inside the floor' wording must not coexist. (2) Use the confirm config exactly: --bf16, --device auto, --max-ans 8, same --data and --vocab; omit --final-eval (it is store_true; 'off' is an argparse error); --log-every 1 for the 200-step bitwise stage and 20 for Stage 2; a frozen code copy so the hashes name the tested code. Per-step losses at --log-every 1 are single-step values; the 500-step-mean final_train_loss is not a per-step number. (3) Add the provenance logging first (torch, CUDA, cuDNN, GPU, OS, ledger/train/data hashes, manifest hash, nvidia-smi sample) because none exists in any RESULT.json. (4) Floors are shape-specific: name q33 (8 rounds, 9 registers, 27 slots) vs the 8a B2 shape (12 rounds, 36 registers, 106 slots) on every number. (5) Tier 1 must be the G2 test as worded in 8A-SPEC section 17 (loss and gradients, 1e-5 relative, fp32/fp64 CPU, same predictions on 1,000 named dev rows), not parameters after 5 AdamW steps. (6) Tier 0 hash must cover gold targets and w_row, not just batch tensors. (7) Include planted controls: a known-equal edit (wider padding) must pass and a known-different edit (shuffled order or a one-slot remap error) must fail. (8) Test the 'same card state' assumption directly with one rerun under a co-tenant and log nvidia-smi; do not assume it. (9) Report, do not claim, any dev-score number; tell Ben a build-time equivalence check makes no score claim and ask him to confirm that reading of rule 4. (10) Ask for claims labelled shown / suggested / untested; keep B2 card-experiment claims separate from the village model; one change at a time; and give Ben (a high-school senior) a plain summary: 'run the same thing twice on the same GPU and see whether the two runs match exactly; if yes, speed rewrites can be proved correct in minutes; if no, we learn how close is close enough before we use it'. (11) Cost accounting: Stages 0-1 are minutes and must be slotted ahead of queue 39 or into a gap; Stage 2 with 5 reference pairs plus 2 held-out pairs at 1,000 steps (about 2-4 min each at the shown 4-8.5 updates/s) is roughly 0.5-1 h on the shared card (suggested); the full 24k calibration pairs are the only expensive part and are optional until a Tier 2 edit actually exists. (12) Rank this behind the one-step profile and the par-1/2/3 throughput test; it is infrastructure with no speedup of its own, and its value is realised only when a speed edit (G2 slot sizing, host-side rewrite, compile) is built. Also state the fast-sleep import caveat (collate, to_device, lr_at, execute) so speed edits do not leak unchecked into the deployed sleep path.

plan.title: Same-config rerun floor and per-batch equivalence gate (D7 revised)
plan.ben_line: We want B2 to train faster without changing what it learns, so first we measure how much one training run differs from an identical run on the same machine. A speed change is accepted only if its math stays inside that measured closeness, checked on fixed batches in minutes instead of by retraining for hours.
plan.question: Can a measured same-config rerun floor, taken per batch (loss and every gradient tensor, compared norm-wise, with no optimizer step), plus a bitwise check for host-side edits and two planted controls, certify that a B2 speed rewrite leaves the math unchanged, with a measured false-reject rate on held-out batches, before any 6-seed score run?
plan.one_change: Infrastructure only: no model change and no score claim. Add provenance and full-precision per-step logging to train.py, then build one per-batch test that measures same-config GPU and CPU reruns, fixes the bars from floor batches, and checks them on held-out batches and planted controls. This replaces the trajectory gate in the direction (every one of 50 logged points within 2x the max of 5 same-config pairs), which rejects identical-math edits far too often in a model-based Monte Carlo (see null_risk).
arms: Stage 0, CPU fp32: B2 config (model ledger, copy true), seed 200, batch 256, 20 steps, two separate processes with the same code. Expected bit-equal (suggested). Do not use in-process reruns: progparse._CACHE (progparse.py line 185) is a module-level dict and would be shared between the two runs.

Stage 1, PC GPU: seed 200, confirm flags (bf16, device auto, max-ans 8, batch 256, lr 1e-3), 200 steps, full-precision loss at every step. Run A, then run B back to back; run C under a co-tenant with nvidia-smi sampled every 5 s; run D with a new --deterministic flag (use_deterministic_algorithms True, CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG=:4096:8, cudnn.deterministic) that records any op that raises. Nothing is patched.

Stage 2, PC GPU, no training and no optimizer step: the same batch goes through forward and backward twice on the same code. Floor batches 0-99 and held-out batches 100-199, taken from the seed-200 shuffled order of training rows only.

(ii) A differs from B: report the first differing step and its size; no bitwise GPU claim; use Stages 2-3 only. (iii) A equals B but C differs: card state matters; every later comparison logs nvidia-smi and runs under the same co-tenant state. (iv) D raises on op X: record X, patch nothing, rely on Stages 2-3. Tier 1 (math-level edits such as per-batch slot sizing or padding width; CPU): per pool batch and per tensor, norm-wise relative difference ||ref - edit|| / ||ref|| for the loss and every pre-optimizer gradient (if ||ref|| < 1e-12, use the absolute difference, bar 1e-12). Bars: fp64 at most 1e-8; fp32 at most 1e-5. Predictions on the 1,000 named dev rows: 0 changed. The elementwise maximum is reported as a diagnostic only.

Tier 2 (GPU float-order edits such as torch.compile, fused kernels, reordered sums; per batch, no optimizer step): floor = the per-tensor norm-wise loss and gradient differences between two same-code runs on floor batches 0-99. Bar = max(10 x the 99th percentile of those floor values, 1e-6), fixed now. Null mark: 0 of the 100 held-out batches (100-199) exceed the bar on any tensor (exact 95% upper bound on the false-reject rate is about 3 percent). Power mark: the remap-error control exceeds the bar on at least 1 held-out batch. Known-equal control (padding 81 vs 161): 0 of 100 exceed. The 1e-3 perturbation is reported as a power number only. The 200-step curve check in the direction is dropped: it has no measured floor.

Tier 3 (batch composition, length bucketing, packing, data order, lr schedule, --minutes changes, or any claim that scores are unchanged): rule 4, six paired seeds (see confirm). Tiers 0 to 2 certify math, not scores.

plan.proved_wrong: The method is wrong if any of these holds: (a) Stage 0 CPU reruns in separate processes are not bit-equal after the logging fix (the CPU reference cannot be used). (c) The known-equal padding control exceeds the Tier 2 bar on any held-out batch, or fails the Tier 1 fp32 bar on any pool batch (the bar or the metric is wrong). (d) Same-code GPU reruns differ by more than 1e-4 norm-wise on the largest tensor (float noise then exceeds any usable bar, so no GPU float-order edit can be certified this way). plan.null_risk: Yes, in three places, and the plan must avoid each. (1) Shown in this review by a Monte Carlo (model-based, not measured on B2): the direction's trajectory gate rejects an exchangeable identical-math edit at a per-point rate of 2.5 percent (analytic, half-normal, 2x max of 5 pairs), and over 50 logged points at 71 percent if points were independent, 48 percent for an AR(1) rho 0.9 Gaussian, and 82 percent for Student-t(3) (4000 trials). At 3x the per-point rate is 0.5 percent and the 50-point rate is 16 percent (rho 0.9). A single pre-registered scalar (mean of the 50 deviations, 2x max of 5) rejects about 0.1 percent at rho 0.9 but has only 4 to 17 percent power against 1.5x to 2x drifts. So the trajectory gate is dropped. (2) Shown in a numpy test of pure float reordering on random 64x256 dot products (this review, not B2 gradients): the elementwise max relative difference exceeded 1e-5 in 53.5 percent of 200 trials (median 1.1e-5), so the sealed G2 wording fails with no real change about half the time; the norm-wise difference had median 3e-7 and fp64 elementwise was about 2e-14. (3) Shown in RESULT.json files: the same seed and config gave final training loss 0.0210 (PC, results/33-pc-confirm-b2/B2_s200), 0.0168 (rented, results/40-egw-s200/B2V_s200) and 0.0128 (rented, first-look-10m-results/B2_s200), so trajectories diverge widely; two held-out pairs cannot measure a 3 percent false-reject rate, but 100 held-out batches can. final.why: The fixed CPU-first plan is sound and breaks no rule: it is a build-time check with no model change and no score claim, and it uses no GPU until a speed edit exists. I re-checked the code facts it relies on (shown). `--final-eval` is `store_true` (train.py:121). No determinism flag exists in train.py. `scatter_add_` sits at ledger.py:248. `progparse._CACHE` is a module-level dict (progparse.py:185). test_harness.py checks `final_train_loss` for plain_tf only, in one process on CPU. fast-sleep imports `collate`, `to_device` and `lr_at` (sleep.py:12-14). It is not worth running now because nothing is built yet to gate it: no profile or par-1/2/3 test has run (untested), so which edit comes first is unknown. If the first edit is a host-side rewrite, bit-equal batches and targets (Tier 0) already settle it with no GPU floor. If it is G2 slot sizing, 8A-SPEC already seals its own 1e-5 test (suggested). The GPU floor matters only for compile, CUDA-graph or fused-kernel edits, and the CPU harness is small enough to write with the first real edit. One piece is worth doing now: write the provenance fields (torch, CUDA, GPU, code and data hashes, `--max-ans`) into RESULT.json. It costs almost nothing and removes the "which box and which code" confound that blurs the same-seed comparisons today (shown: seeds 200/201 differ by +0.48/+0.12 pooled-5 with no versions or hashes recorded).
final.ben_line: Run the same speed-up check on fixed test batches before and after a code change so we can prove a faster version does the same math in minutes instead of retraining for hours, but only build it once we have an actual speed change to check, and start by writing down which GPU, software versions and code each run used.
